TEE LIG TlTtli):73l3. High o'er the black-backed Skerries, and far To the westward hills, and the eastward sea, I shift my light, like a twinkling star, With ever a star's sweet constancy. 'They wait for me when the night comes down, And the slow sun falls in his death divine ; Then, braving the black night's gathering frown, With ruby and diamond blaze—l shine! There is war at my feet, where the black rocks break Tbe thunderous snows of the rising sea; ShPre is peace, above, when the stars are awake. Keeping their night-long watch with me. I care not a jot for the roar of the surge, The wrath is the sea's—the victory mine ! As over Its breadth, to the farthest verge, Unwavering and ntitired— I shine! First on my brow comes the pearly light. Dimming my lamp in the new-born day. One long, last look to left and right, And I rest from my toll,—for the broad sea-way Grows bright with the smile and blush of the sky, All incandeacent and opaline. I rest—but the loveliest day will die,— Again in its last wan sbadovrs—l shine! When the night is black, and the wind is loud, And danger is hidden, and peril abroad, The seaman leapton the swaying shroud: His e 3 e is on me, and his hope In God! Alone, in the darkness, any blood-red eye Yeets his, end he hauls his groping line. "'A point to nor'ard !" I bear him cry. Be goes with a b'essing, and still—l shine While standing afore in the summer sun, I sometimes have visions and drearn3 of any own, Of long-life voyages just begun, And rocks unnoticed, and shoals unkrown ; And I would that men and women would mark The duty done by Mil lamp of mine; For many a life is lost in the dark, And few on earth are the lights that shine! —Good Words. Foot aud mouth disease has been conveyed to Dublin by a shorthorn ball purchased by Lord Larbury in Weetmorlend, and admitted into Ireland by special permission from the Lord Lieutenant. The animal WAS travelled in a horse•box to Liverpool, and special precautions taken in every way. One of the successful dairymen of Wisconsin, at the late meeting of the dairymen of that State, expressed himself as strongly in favour of winter dairying, and had Statistics to chow that he was right. Good care, he said, would produce as much milk from a cow in winter as in summer. The gross weight might not be as great, but the essential milk qualities, without the water, would average up at well. flown KREP.—CARROTS.—A few pulped carrots, swedes, and mangels, say a peck to a horse each day, mixed with chaff, afford a wholesome and nutritious food for cart horses, far more go than staffing them with corn, thereby making them liable to diseases of a- very hurtful character. No farm should be without an acre of carrots; no crop pays so well, often producing from 15 to 20 tone per acre, and ;hey are the best food for horses and milking cows. Prof. L. B. Artold says the points in favour of dairying are—First, a dairy farm coots ten per cent. lees to operate than grairogro wing or mixed agriculture; second, the annual returns average a little more than other branches; third, prlees are nearer eniform and more reliable; fourth. dairy- ing exhausts the soil less ; fiftb, it is more secure against changes in the saver:, since the dairyman does not suffer PO much from wet and frost and varying maser's, and he can, if prudent, protect against drought. The year 1882 has been the most guecessful one yet re- corded in the annals ef the Holywell herd of white pigs, the property of Mr. Sanders Spencer. The sales of boars and sows for breeding purposes have made the very large total of 283, the animals having been distributed pretty well over the known world. The Holly well Manor herd has not been represented at any of the rummer shows, Mr. Seeders Spen- cer having earned all the reputation hecares for of that kind, and he now finds the resources of his herd taxed to the utmeet in supplying the home and foreign denaande made upon it. A report by M. Be:Ad to the Permanent Committee of , Economy and Rural Legislation, appointed by the Society of French Agriculturists, enumerates the seven chief griev- ances of agricuhaere as being—(l) that it his not equal re- preeentation with Industry, in tied the consultative chem. bets are appointed by the prefects, and cannot claim redress from Government ; (2) that the cost of load tranefer is ex. cES3iVe ; (3, that it pays more than its fair Aare of icopesta (4) that it pays taxes when it yields no revenue; (5) that , agriculture pays more than its share of the cost of thel ineintenance of roads; (6) that it does riot eojoy equality] before the Cu4toles ; and (1) 23 regards reeietretion. Upon this report the society recomenerds legielation with the view of aboliehlag the icequelities suffered by agriculture in its capacity of chief of Industries. In die.cut.ine the general subject of dairying, Dr. Start°. vent says—.' The fact is true that the breed is more impor- tent than tee food. Milk ie manufactured. The milk is made from the tio2ues of the cow, and by her own functions, and it is not strained through her. The sources of the milk supplying each teat are wholly separate, and the milk often differs materially in composition. Evidence shows that the milk-producing power is inherited and may be changed or inc.eased by breeding. The amount of croon does not indi- cate the value of a cow for butter. Sometimes cows with little cream surpass in butter a cow producing more cream. Toe amount of cream diffets in the same cow. I had a cow which averaged day after day from 10 to 12 per cent of cream. One day she produced 60 per cent. of cream: One experiment showed a difference of hotel 24 to 42 per cent. of cream in different teats at the same milking. So far as I know there Is no way of determining the batter quality of milk except the churn." TIMELY PREPARATIONS —A thorough inspection of the &puck of bedding plants intended for the summer garden should be made now, and where the nu ober of any particu- lar variety is deficient, means should be at once taken to in. crease it by propagation either by seeds or cuttings. If by cuttings it is advisable in most cases before taking them off. to subject the Ocoee to .a slightly-increased temprreture, so as to stimulate growth beforehand. The cuttings will then strike with much greater freedom and certainty. If the stock of plants has been stored in cold pits or houses through the winter, the temperature of.a vinery or peach-house just started will afford them the proper temperature and other conditions requisite to excite growth. The cattings should be placed in a brisk bottom heat in the propagating house, but if there is not the convenience of this molt useful struc- ture, a common dung bed and frame will answer the-purpose admirably, provided the dung has been previously prepared by throwing it together, with the addition of a few oak or chestnut leave!, well mixing and turnieg it three or four times within the space of a fortnight, and then built evenly and firmly to the required size and the frame placed noon it. A little sawdust, ashes, or Any similar material suitable for plunging the pots in is all that is required. In a few days efter garde the rank stream will have pissed off, and the cuttings may be introduced. TIOUSEIIOLD PETS.
Does —Tea Pl:Yd.—This la a favourite breed of dogs .with

the ladies, and it is seldom that anyone who pretends to occupy a leading place in fashionable society is without a pug dog. As carriage pets they are much to be preferred to terrierF, as they are quieter and not given to yelping as are too many of their noisy brethren. The Dutch claim the honour of their introduction into Europe, and during the reign of William 11l they were great favourites, so that the fashion for keeping them which now exists is only a re- newal of that existing nearly 200 years ago. Tbey are es- sentially pet dogs, and quite useless for watchers, even where a small amount of bravery is required, as they in. variably show the white feather, though the combatant is on7v a fcwi or a naggy young terrier. Thus they are suit. able for ladies who desire above all to lead a quiet life, and as they Are cap.ble of forming strong attachments we do not wonder at their becoming great favourites. They are, Ito. ever, often indolent and stupid, but this is more the fault of their owLers than of the dogs themselves, for if pro- perly fed and exercised, they are lively and cheerful, but if they have an abundance of rich food and are allowed to snooze nearly all day in front of the the, or on the lap of their owner, they are both stupid and indolent. A Pug to be kept in health and condition, should be sparingly fed and judiciously exercised, then it will be a source of pleasure to its owner. The points of a pug have been defined as fol- lows :—The head, round and moderately large (a small head is a great fault) ; the face, short and square at the noee; the cheeks, muscular and full; the tongue. large, and there, are some who like to see a little of it protrude; the ears thin, small, and black, and lie close to the face; eyes, brown, full, and gentle in their glance; and a mole in each cheek with three hairs in each, which should be black. The mask and wrinkles should be black, as should the vent. All pugs have a black stripe down the middle of the back, but it is more clearly defined in some varieties than others. The colour may be a rich golden shade or a cool gray, and the coat, elope, ehort, and shiney. The tail is closely curled, lying flat against the side, the hair of it rough and rather I,mor than the half on the body, which is very thick, mus- cular, and cobby. The cheat is round and wide, the quarters ard loiai full and muscular, with a strong full neck, but no h.lnk-f•T WTI. The legs are straight and small boned; the f e*, hare or ea' shaped, with black nails. Pugs vary in e'ze, but the smaller they are the more they are admired, itd the whole appearance ehould be thoroughly lumen- triral.

I MAK''G AN .44at1tultr5t.--The efzs of the aquarium to be I m ade will, of covet, depend partially upon the amount of ' ccoey which it is thought desirable to spend upon it, and I thfon tipsn the pint were It il9 be put, The einipleet end leset inpensoie and sooneat fitted tip is the bell o.re, whl,:h CM be bought very reasonably of any glass merchant, tied is made ha mm 7 AiZes. When this is placed upon a nice stand and has a neat cover, it makes a very pretty orna- ment, and will look well in any place. This is, however, limited in sfze, as the glass bowls cannot be made very large, fur they would not then be capable of supporting a great body of water In them. When a larger one is wished for, and space not so much an object, nor yet cost, an oblong tank may be selted, and it can be made almost any size. For fresh water the framework may be made of wood, zinc, iron, or glare pillars, with glees aides; but for durability and strength, we prefer those made of slate, and a glass front, i e., slate bottom, back, and ends, or, if preferred, both front and back can be of glass. When not made in this way, the bottom should be lined either with glass or slate, and it La better to embed this in cement A little extra cost is well spent at first, as wood is very unserviceable, and when it begins to leak is not at all catty to repair. The shape can be left to the discretion of the maker, and can be square, oblong, octagonal, or, in feet to fit any place, so long as the internal arrangements are looked after. It reay be as well here to refer to the position of the aquarium, as that will in many cues have much to do with its shape. Generally we find such things in front of a window, and, where this is the case, it is beet to have it in one facing the east, where it will get the morning sun for two or three hours. If this cannot be done, and a southern window has to be taken, then shade is necessary during the middle of the day, as the sun is then much too hot. A little sun is needed, and on this account many aquariums in rooms facing the north or west do not succeed, much to the surprise of their ownrrs. It must be borne in mind that the great point is to keep the temperature as even as possible, not to allow it to fail below 45 or rise above 65 degrees. Of course. this entails care and watchfulness, but these add to the in- terest aed pleasure of the pursuit. If there was no trouble Involved, there would be little enjoyment got out of it. ID summer. temperature can be reduced by opening the win- dow, and in winter increased by drawing the aquarium into the ream. !Joon no account must it be allowed to freeze, or , the tank will probably burst, a disaster which would not only be a lota, but do a great amount of damage to carpets, ,tc., and even If it doea not burst, the fish and plants will drool) and d,le.. Light and heat need to be regulated, so far 29 their Run:union to the tank is concerned. With slate Itanke, this has already been provided for; but with bell glasses, or tanke in which the sides are entirely of glass. thin green paper should be pasted over all the glass except the front, np to the water lice. By this means the light is subdued, and the objects in the aquarium will always pre- sent a better and more natural appearance if the light is admitted at the top. The admission of light through the opposite end or side of a tank will induce an excessive growth of vegetat'on, and cause the accumulation of a green Clo: on the front that will in a short time obscure the con- tee's from view. FitIGHTPNING TUF.SPASSISRS.--In tee "Traditions of Edinburgh," we are told that after he had finished his plea- sure-grounds, Mr. Ross was much enraged by nightly tree. passers, and advertised spring-guns and mamtraps without avail. At las; he conceived the idea of procuring a human leg from the Royal Infirmary, and dressing it up with a stocking, shoe, and buckle, sent it through the town, borne aloft by the crier; proclaiming that "It had been found last night in Mr. Walter Rose's policy at Stockbridge, and offer- ing to restore it to the disconsolate o veer." After this, no 1 one attempted to break into his grounds.—Ofd and /Veto Edinburgh. Edale is a primitive seclusion in the midmost depths of "The _Peak," in Derbyshire. The inhabitants are all of the roughest type, and keep as much as possible out of the sight Of strangers. A story is told of one of them who, some fifty years ago, was so aiventureus as to make a jsurney to Sheffield, about twenty miles distant. When he set off to return it was raining hard, and his host lent him an umbrella —opening it himself in order to save his friend all possible trouble. A fortnight afterwards this man of Edale was seen to return in the finest possible weather, but with the trek:retie still op. " Why," he explained, "we bud A peck o' troubl-s wi' on. There wasn't a doorway ha the village we could get 'an through, so we tethered 'en in a field." BIBERNATION.—The hat teethes another and most valu- able letson in the economy of animal life. The pep! Nei learned that it feeds exclusively on flying insert.. Hue then is it to live during the winter months, when insects have vanished? There is nothing for it but death by starvation, unless it should possess some propeny not shifted by the generality of animals, and which can make it indepen- e'en% et food until ehe ineects come out again. This property 713 called hibernation, and a Most remarkable and unee,ceuel. We property it is. In the later weeks of the autumn, the animal accumulates a large supply of fat, especial:y in the Interior of the body. As soon as the colder days of ap- proaching winter make themselves felt, the bat seeks out some retired spot, such as the trunk of a hollow tree, a cre- vice in a rock, or some old building, where it will not be disturbed. It then hangs itself up by the hooked claws of Its hind feet, wraps its wings round its body, and passes into a eteite-of lethargy. Respiration ceases altogether, and so doe,l digestion, while the heart only gives a feeble beat once in each second, Just enough to keep the blood circulat- ing. Scarcely any waste of the tissues takes place, and the fat which has been stored up is the body affords sufficient nourishment to keep the creature alive, though net sensible, through the whole of the winter. The hedgehog, squirrel, and demonse are partially susceptible of hibernation, but the bat is the ,only perfect hibernator which inhabits the , country. Not only does it hibernate in the winter, but it Passes into this lethargy once in every day, even in the midst of summer.---" My Back-Yard Zoo" in Good Words. A. and Galpin, and an interesting description is given this month of the Jay, from which we cull the following:— " Few birds have obtained such an unenviable notoriety as the Jay. Equally with the Magpie abhorred by tho hus- bandman, farmer, and gamekeeper. The Jay, in the reign of George It, was conaidered such a desperate character, that an Act of Parliament was passed empowering certain authorities to pay a reward of threepence pr head for every slaughtered bird. Doubtless this had the effect of lessening the number, for although the Jay is still common to almost all parts of England, it is not what may be termed plentiful. This, too, is because, like most of the tribe, Jays show a preference for certain localities, though without any ap- parent reason, as the regions they affect are generally low waste lands, without the means of subsistence that a neigh- bouring fertile locality would obviously afford. . . The home of tbe Jay is generally pitched in wood, or in pier* tient, known 23 c Tees, sheee, Or spinneys, and from these ventage-grounds this bird lays all the surrounding country under tribute. The food includes, besides insects and worms, the eggs and young of small birds, trait such a cherries, pets and such like vegetables, anything in the shape of corn or grain; indeed, keepers of preserves have to be specially watchful to see that the Indian corn cud other food placsd for the game is not eaten by the Jays. Doubtless the Jay has his good qualities, and possibly did ha not eat the insects they wpuld demolish more than he does; but the gun of the gamekeeper and the trap of the husbandman are as much directed against the Jay as the Magpie. . . . Gamekeepers often find Jays to be useful detectives, since their continuous chattering is known to determine the presence of earns adverse power in the wood wherein they wished to be sole depredators. . . . When taken young the Jay makes a nice pet, for his plumage is more beautiful than any of his genus. Even the Magpie cannot vie with the Jay in delicacy of colouring or effective centast. . . . The note of the Jay is far from pleasing, being a retedly•delivered, harsh sort of chatter. Some naturalists have made mention of its song, but say it can- not be heard at any distance. The bird, however, may with patience be taught to talk in almost equal degree with the Magpie, and somewhat in advance of the Sterling. Its powers of mimicry are unwetally great, as it will imitate extraordinary sounds very rapidly, and seems to take a pleasure in doing so. It is singular that, like many other birds with three peculiarities, the Jay is naturally inqeisi- tive and somswhat mischievous, and should, therefore, be carefully watched."

The council of the Durhem Miners' Association agreed on Saturday to propose to the coalowners to work the collieries five days per week. . At a mass meeting of Ferest of Dean miners on Saturday, it was decided to appeal to the South Wales men not to work more than eight hours per day. At a conference of the representatives of 28,000 miners of South Yorkshire, at Barnsley, on Monday, it was decided to abide by the decision of the Manchester Conference on the 27th inst. as to the restriction of output. A deputation of Northumberland miners, headed by Mr. T. Burt, M P., waited on the coalowners at a meeting in Newcastle on Saturday, when it was resolved to leave the questien of the future sliding scale for the adjustment of wages to a joint committee of masters and men. The colliers employed at the Flint Colliery Company's extensive works ceased operations- on Saturday in conse- quence of the intention of the proprietors to close the col- liery at once. The company has the power of raising nearly 1,000 tons of coal weekly, and have coal mines under a sur- face area of about 820 acres. The stoppage of the work.° will seriously affect the trade of Flint. BILLS OF SALE AND FAILURES—In the week ending February 10, 1883, there were 239 bills of sale in England and Wales, a decreased 786 over those of the corresponding period last year ; and the failures gazetted numbered 214, a decrease of 4. The totals for portion of year to February 10, 1883, are bile of sale registered for England and Wales, 1,451, a decrease of 4.471 the failures gazetted number 1,292, an increase of 30.—Stubbs' Mercantile Gazette. REDUCED WAGES IN THE SHEFFIELD TRADES.—An important meeting of the Manufacturers' Association was held in Sheffield, on Tuesday. The masters had decided to reduce the wages of the workmen 10 per cent., but the men engaged in one of the most extensive of the hardware trades strongly objected. The meeting decided to pry a Uniform wage no longer, but that each firm should make its own terms with the men. The eff,ct is that large bowies will -for the present pay 10 per cent. less. THE OUTPUT OF COAL IN LANCASHIRE AND CHESUIRE. —On Wednesday a largely attended conference of delegates, representing-49,000 miners in Lancashire and Cheshire, was held at the Miners' Hall, Wigan, under the presidency of Mr. S. 'Woode,of Park-lane. Short reports were read from districts on the question cf restricting output, and it was ceneidered that on the whole they were very encouraging. After discussion, it was agreed that the conference adhere to the resolution pissed at the Leeds conference to work eight hours Pet der and five days per week, cad they recommended the same to the forthcoming conference at Manchester. Another conference will be called if necess3ry. THE LANCASHIRE ,IRON TRADE.— The condition of the iron market continues very unsatisfactory, with the business offering of the most limited description, and a persistent effort on the part of buyers to pull down prices still further. In pig iron there were no parcels of any weight changing hands on Tuesday, as buyers even where they had small orders to place were not disposed te come up to makers' prices, Whilst makers seemed to have set their faces agalnst further concessions. For Lancashire pig iron inquiries have been very small at abut Is per ton under makers' rates, and in district brands where any sales are reported they are a few lots of foundry. Quoted rates remein about as under ' Lancashire forge and foundry. 443 6d to 475; Lincolneldie, 46s to 485 And Derbyshire 48s 631 to 50s, less 21 delivered cqtial to Manchester. In the finished iron market merchants are:" bearing" in a most-determined manner, and in some casts are offering at 2s 61 par ton under the lowest possible makers' prices. There ere plenty of sellers of bars at £6 5s per ton delivered into the Manchester district, although. makers ask more. , THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADF.—The somewhat better tore which has been noticeable in the coal trade of this dis• trict since the present month set in is b.,ing maintained. The restriction of the output has no doubt tended in a limited measure to affect supplies, and in some cases collieries have (bend it difficult to keep up with their orders; but generally it has not been materially felt, and there ie still an abundance of coal offering in the markets. Tile downward tendency in prices appears for the present to hive been checked, eml although there is a good deal of low selling, there is less disposition to give way upon quoted rates to secure orders. The market generally may be said to be steady, with quotations at the pit mouth averaging abut 103 for the beet sorts of house coal, 7s 61 to 8s for seconds, 6s 6d to Is for common, 5s 61 to 64-for steam and forgo 'coals, 5s to 5s 3d for burgy, and 3e 64 to 4s for ordinary qualities of slack. The demand for shipment shows improvement. Liverpool or Garston docks not fetching more than 7s 91 to Sc with house fire qualities averaging Os 3d to Os 61 per ton: THE LABora MARXET.—This market is brisk, although the agitation in reference to wages and time, to a certain extent, interferes with it. Building and railway contracts continue to be placed, and there is plenty of work for nav- vies and all who are able to assist in constructing railways, docks, and trernways. At Barneley the linen trade continues quiet, as the home demand is not improved. At Barrow-in- Furness steel makers are busy, and makers of hematite iron are fairly employed. In Bermondsey the tanners and cur- riers are increasing their number of employes. At Bir- mingham there is a moderate dem Ind for goods for Austra- lia and New Zealand; and in tools for engineers there is a good demand. At Darlington iron trade is slack. At the Hartlepools ebippine, is brisk, but coal trade is quiet. At Hannay the pottery industry is rather quiet. At Newcastle- on-Tyne shipbuilders are busy, and builders have orders in hand enough to occupf them for the beat part of the year. In South Shropshire the iron' trade continues steady. At Sheffield the cutlery and hardware trade is increasing, but but 13ess“ner and crucible steel trade is falling off. At Sunderland 'shipbuilders are very busy. At Wolverhatnpe ton orders have this week come in freely, and many firms have enough work for the next three months. In the textile trades, although there are some disputes in reference to wages, we mey say that work is fairly abundant. At Brad- ford there ieea fair demand for Botanies and mohair, and moderate business in prices for home demand. At Dundee orders for linen are coming in freely. At ELlifax the manufacturers are fairly busy on orders, the price of which is low. At Huddersfield all branches of cloth trade are quiet. Best worsteds and cheao tweeds are in demand. Canadian orders increasing, and shipments to America also improving. At Kidderminster, cerp'et trade a fair demand. At Leeds, cheap cloths quiet. A slight improvement in special coatings for shipment. At Leicester hosiers are busy, and the beot and shoe trade ii improving. At Man- chester the cloth trade is improving. Yarns are steady. At Nottengham. a Lair trade in hosiery. The curtain trads is brisk, wed bobbin netts in good demand.—Labour News. •

DEATH OF RICHARD WAGNER.—The death is announced at Venice, on Tuesdoy, of Richard Wagner, the composer, at the age of 70. Most of deceased's operas were produced at Dresden. In 1865 Wagner was director of the London Phil. harmonic Society. His pamphlet, "Judaism in Music," 1869, aroused considerable discussion. In 1872 he laid at Bairenth the foundation stone of a theatre, in which his works were perforated in 1876. His works were first intro- duced in London in February, 1873. " Lehengrin " was performed in 1875, " Pannhauser "in 1876. The "Ring des Niebelungen,".in four parts, was performed at Baireuth in 1876 in the presence of several crowned heads, and again in ISBI at Berlin.

SECRET Somery TYRANNY.—A painful sensation has been cense(' at Vienna by a suicide which has taken place at Prague, and which has led to an extraordinary disclosure. The victim WAS a glover's apprentice, ahout eighteen years of age, who had hanged himself in his chamber. In expla- nation of his conduct the deceased,had left a letter on his table. It was addressed to his parents, and in it he stated that be had been selected by a Secret society to take the life of one of the chief officer of the police of the city—Police- director Steipkal. He had committed suicide in order to evade the performance of this tisk. If he had not carried out the behests of the secret organization the writer states that he would himself have been assass'nated by his col- , Icergere. Marshal Serrano and the members of the "Dynastic Left" held a meeting on Monday, and resolved to begin an "energetic policy" in opposition to the Government. The Marshal contradicted the report of his retirement from the leadership of the party. Some of the Madrid journals are ' much excited by the prospect of 'encountering an "English opposition" in Morocco, where the Spaniards hope to acquire a "preponderating" influence. .El Correo warns the Government of Morocco that it§ independence would be seriously threatened if-it were to allow England to obtain a firm footing in Morocco. • The warning is, of course, intended as against England, since it can scarcely be supposed that Spain would succeed in subverting the independence of a country in which we had " obtained a firm footing ;" but the alarm of El Correo is groundless. GREAT ROBBERY OF SPECIE IN AMERICA.—A shipMent of £lOO,OOO (Ms, was made by the sub-treasury in New York to the United Statet fleet on the Pacific, by the steamer City of Para, which arrived at Asp!niyall on the 29th Dec. The money, American gold coin, was packed in two small kegs, weighing about 200Ihs. each. They were received in Panama the same evening, and stored_ for safe keeping.in the Panama Railroad Company's vault. elivery was not made until the let of January, when, on the vault being opened, it was diitovered that one keg was Missing. No locks had been broken. Evidence was found that the keg had ben opened in the freight-house, but neither the keg nor any vestige thereof, nor its dontentS, could be discovered after a long and careful search. Several arrests have been male, but nothing positive his yet been ascertained to throw lieht on the mysterious affair.. . .

Tun Exrcrr.stoN BILL.—The debtte on the Pretenders Expulsion Bill was resumed in the French Senate on Mon- day. On a division the House resolved by 170 votes to 115 to ,pass to the discussion of the articles of the bill. The Minister of Justice announced that the Government had agreed to abandon the bill passed by the Chamber, and to accept a counter proposal to the effect that a decree of the President of the Republic, given at a Council of :Ministers, should be sufficient for the expulsion of princes whose acts compromised the safety of the State This proposition was rejected, as also was Article I. of the Ministerial bill; and the House. by 165 votes to 127, adopted a proposal of M. Waddington declaring that any prince who shall commit any act in furtherance of his pretensions to the 'throne of France, or engage in manifestations tending to affect the safety of.the State, shall be punished by banishment from French territory, the prosecw ion to take place before the Court of Assizes or before the Senate sitting as a High Court of Justice.

div.head: DREIDFUL lIIURPER IN CHESHIRE
div.p: DREIDFUL lIIURPER IN CHESHIRE

In the early part of yesterday (Friday) afternoon week, a terrible tragedy was committed. at Smallwood, near S oid- bach, Cheshire. It wins out to be one of the most dreadful outrages that has been perpetrated in the locality for many years, although it has not, as at first reported, resulted in the death of both persons attacked. Thomas Earlarn, the owner of the house in which the tragedy was enacted, was killed outright, but the woman, at first said to be Mrs. Earlam, but who was his housekeeper, is still alive. Her injuries are, however, of such a serious nature that she cannot possibly recover. She has been in an unconscious slate since. The house (which was used by the owner mainly for keeping lodgers) is situate on the road from Congleton to Arclid. It stands by itself, and is a low, dilapidated building. Some of the receipts found in the deceased's desk relating to the rent date as far back as 1770. The district is very thinly populated, the nearest house being a hundred yards off. It is half a mile from the village church, and altogether its position is such that a tragedy of the kind enacted might have remained undiscovered for hours. The house is a ricketty old building,vrith only three bedrooms 'Flie ceiling is not higher than seven feet, and the flows of the bedrooms are so insecure that it would be dangerous for any large number of persons to venture upstairs, although one of the lodgers has stated tbat he had seen as many as 17 persons sleeping in the rooms. The township of Small- wood is in the Conreleton Union, in the hundred of Middle- wich, and has a scattered population of 602 persons, chiefly engaged in agriculture. The nearest postal telegraph station is Congletou, four miles off. It appears that on the day named a man named Jack came to the house and asked for lodgings, which he .got. There were then living at the house Earlarn and his housekeeper, who is named Moran, and who had lived with him 30 years; a woman named Lavinia Shannon; a rag and bone gatherer, named John Slack; and two man named Sampy and Jones. The latter was apprehended and lodged in Congleton Gaol on suspicion, but has since been released. Earlam was asked by one of the lodgers if he knew anything of Jack, and he said he thought he was a potato dealer, and that he had lodged at the house two years before. During his stay he did nothing but beg from house to house in the district. On the morn- ing of -the day on which the murder was committed Slack says he left Jack in the house at half-past nine o'clock, the other lodgers having then left. illY,ut noon a boy saw Jack look in at one of the windows, and it is supposed he then entered and committed the deed. The murder appears to have been perpetrated with a joiner's hammer, which was found near with blood on it. The walls are all bespattered with blood, so are several articles of furniture. In the back kitchen, a kind of coal cellar, the woman was found in two pools of blood. Earlam's body was found in the kitchen near the fireplace, where he usually sat. He was evidently struck from behind, and killed almost instantaneously, nil head being battered in. Then the murderer appears to have stepped over his body, the passage .between the two rooms being very narrow, and dealt with his other victim, Moran, who was all but blind. She is fearfolly mutiTated about the head and face, and has not spoken since. Dr. Latham, of Sandbach, is in attendance, but he has little hope of her recovery. Earl-mm's chin and jawbone are broken, and one part of the head is broken in. The lodger, Sampv, who it is said ie com- fortably .off, has missed his bank book and a suit of clothes, and a man was seen to leave the neighbourhood about the time the murder is said to have been committed, carrying a bundle, but no clue of his whereabouts has as yet been ascertained. Jones says he knows nothing of the mur- der, excepting that when, about three o'clock, he went to the house and tried to get in he found the door locked, a most unusual thing, and on forcing an entrance saw the man and woman lying in pools of blood. Earlarn appears to have beersof peculiar.babits, not haying been in bed far 30 years. He always slept on a chair before the firs, and Moran on a sofa near him, the beds being reserved far lodgers. It is not supposed that there was any money in the house, and it is thought that the murderer got no plunder but a suit of. clothes. •

The coroner's inquest on thti body of Eariam was opened on Monday and adjourned. The evidence of a surgeon was that deceased had most probably been struck from behind. The head was frightfully smashed, the boners being broken up into quite a hundred pieces. The police are searching the district for a man named "Jack White," who had lodged in the house for a few days and who is supposed to be the murderer. White was seen to leave the honsoalnut three hours before the murder was diflCOtTred he was carrying a bundle. A policeman met the man about 100 yards from the dwelling just after the ainrd,!r tliT!t have lren committed, and therefore cootl description oi his apPear'aii. has been 11') cribed as of about 35 years of age, 5 fe•-,t 7 inches in of stout build, dark complexion, 11111 whlskers or moustache, slightly pock-marked, wearing brown felt h et, long blue overcoat, and patched cwduroy trowers. Several years ago an old man named Beech, living by himself in a cottage jr, the same village, was murdered under precisely the same circumstances.

div.p: ANrEolev TnotfAlFis" AND TIM NFORO Weir.—The late Anthony Tro!lope, a propos of the independent airs and superior manner assumed by negro servants in the West Indiee, recounts a little scene he had with a young black servant in an hotel in Jamaica. In England, one is apt to think that an extra shilling will go a hno way with boots and chambermaid ; bat in the West Indies it is necessary that these people be treated with dignity. They like fami- liarity, but are averse to ridicule. "Hallo, old fellow, bow about that bath ?" Mr. Trollop.) said cue morning to a lad who had been ordered to see a bath filled for him. He was cleaning boots, and went on as if he had nut heard a word. "I say, bow about that bath?" he continued, but the !ad did not move a muscle. "Pot down those le )otp,sir,and go do as I bid you," " Who you call feller ! YO3 speak to a .zenel. man gcnelmanly, and den he fill de bath." "Jame'," said Trollope, with a polite bow." might I trouble you to leave those boots and sae the bath filled for me ?" " Eec, ear," returning the bow, "genelman go at once."—Lead on Society. 1. TEIAIS OF AS PE CIAL ARTIST.—MS. Johnson, of the Graphic, with his coadjutor, Mr. F. Villiers, has only recently returned from Egypt, where an adventure hap- pened to him which I give here, becanee it illustrates the special's audacious pertinacity and the difficulties with which he ha)) often to contend. Mr. Johnson was attached to the Indian Division, whose advance on Cairo was ex- pected to be smparate from that of the main force under Sir Garnet Woteeley. At the Lest moment the two columns were combined ; when, as the regulations forbade more then one representative of each journal acconapanyirg the force in the field, he became an otetc-at. Alert staff odicere threatened arrest, imprisonment, expulsion tram the coun- try; and the Sdecl LI was caught more than once trying to smuggle himself to Cdro disgul.ed as an officer's servant, and several times he was ignominiously hauled out of hiding in baggage-trucks. At last he got t ) Tel-el-Kehir by crouch- ' ing between trusses of hay in a forage train—where the mosquitos and the heat rendered him totally unrecognis- able. He was thus able to dodge staff offieers and censors; but having no ratiooa of his own, and being unable to claim any from the authorities, he fell into desperate straits. He tells me that he walked all over the field of Tel-el Kebir the day after the battle there "looking for a breakfast," and finding none ; and at last, worn nut, he declared himself late in the afternoon to Sir Garret, who, under the circum- stances, offered him a peat in his train just starting for Cairo. All went well afterwards, and Mr. Villiere being down with the fever, Mr. Johnson took his place and re- mained at Cairo until ordered home. --ilfage Ire cf. Art.

Ths prosecution of Prince Napoleon having entirely collapsed, he has been released. Great damage has bet n c Lased at Cincinnati by a freah outbreak of floods. The country for ten miles around fie town is under water, and the damage is estimated at several million dollars.
A Cairo telegram confirms the r.--port that a body of Egyptian troops had surrendered to the " Faioe Prophet." The situa'ion in the Soudsn daily becomes more threat- ening'.

The Ministerial crisis in France still exists. It is pro- b.:tole that tht interview betweut the Piesilent of the Re- pubic and M. Failie-ts will result in the formation of a Cabinet on the lines of a oompromise amongst the v.rrious Tiranches r)f the 11,publicau party. rith rt, rerenea to the finances of F.4ypt that is kited .% duringth list quarter of ls he revenue rec:iipts came in with a rapidity that exceeded all expßtair.o' ; and as the expenditure has been kept down there is every roon lo be- lieve that there will b 3 no Aldieit on the accounts of the year. According to a Vienna correspondent, Turkey has again appealed to the Powers upsn the Montenegrin frontier ques- tion, requesting their good offices in order to bring about a solution. This appeal has hen made twice before. but without effect, the opinion of the Powers being that the two States oughtto negotiate immediately with one an- other.

PREPARING FOR THE CZAR'S CORONITION.—AIthough the ex tct date in May has not yet been given, it is belived that the Cztr's coronation will take place in the second half of the month. In the meantime vast prep trations are in progress. The construction of temporary theatres and fair- booths, and the fitting up of tile Kremlin with the electric light have already begun at 510300 W. The Consular Treaty between Germany and Servia, a draft of which has been submitted by Prince Bismarck to the Federal Council, contains a provision by whi,.:ll the German Government renounces the exercise of capitulation rights in Servia, anil defines the obligations of Servia con- cerning the surremler of oritninals, at the same time rosary- int the conclusion cf an extradition treaty for a latter period. Sven members of a secret revolutionary band in Bohemia have been arrested at Prague. The object of the conspirators is stated"to have been the realisation of a Nihilist or Social- ist programme. The places of meeting were different public houses in the city, and sometimes a forest on the outskirts of Prague. A number of revolvers and pocket daggers were found on the premises occupied by the persons arrested.

l'rince Napoleon "desires it to be known " that he bases his appeal to the French people on the ground that no national vote has yet quashed tbe plebisicitunt recorded -(shortly be- fore the war with Germany) in favour of the Bonaparte dynasty. He therefore "considers himself entitled to urge that the present rulers of France are governing on the strength of popular apathy and not by popular consent." The Prince states that his son Victor will, if he should be e‘xpElled from France, enter the army of Italy. A Cairo corespondent reports that the Egyptian Govern- ment will shortly issue a new loan for at least £4,000,000, to cover the cost of the indemnity and the expenses of the occupation. Nothing is said as to an English guarantee of this loan, but if it he true that the British Government is about to pledge its credit in order that the tribute to the Sultan may be terminated, it may be supposed that it will either give a similar assistauce towards the floating of the new loan, or that the issue of the loan will he delayed until Egypt's own credit has been strengthened by the termina- tion of the tribute. _ _ _

A correspondent says: —Here is a little piece of infantile ingenuity which may be worth a place. My small nephew was still wearing apparel partaking of the mixed character of boy's and girl's. Hie short gown worried him a great deal; he was anxious to gat a boy's jacket and trousers. Finally, his aunt sent him, as a present, the garments he had so long sighed for. As soon as he wee dressed he went up to his mother, and exclaimed, jyfally," Flow, it is all over! lam a man for ever! There is no danger now that I shall he a girl !" An American map agent was once making( si4 trip in the in- terior of the Island of Cabs, to sell maps, Olien he was at- tacked by highway robbers, who demanded his money. He was more prudent than to carry money in much a country, and they failed in making a haul. "Bat," said our Yankee, "I have splendid maps of Use Wand along with me, which I should like to show you;' and in a twinkling he was off his horse, had a map eat, and explained it so effectually that he sold one le each of the the banditti, pocketed She money, and resumed his journey, better off for the en- counter.

In Mr. John Cordy Jeaffreaon's "Book about the Table" we have this anecdote of the great musical composer Haydn, who iiked to dine alone and eat much. It was his custom to order dinner for five at his favourite hotel, and at the ap- pointed hour to devour the whole banquet. "Serve dinner," he said on'one occasion to a new waiter, who was not aware of the musician's way of sustaining himself "The dinner is ready," returned the waiter, bowing respectfully to the hotel's beet customer, "but, sir' the company, is not come." "Dc gempany!" Haydn retorted, contemptuously. " Pooh ! de gampany ! lam de gompany !" The dinner for five was forthwith put before "de gompany," and not an edible scrap of it found its way back to the kitchen. Domenic Fthes.—Send for an ironmortger or blacksmith, and order him to take the measure of the bottom of your grate, and make you a sheet-iron plate of about one-sixth or an inch in thickness, or even lees, which, if your grate be I large will coat you about two-shillines. Simply lay this on the bottom of the grate, then let your servant lay anti light your fire as usual. It will soon burn up, but you must keep, pretty open the lowest bar, so as to secure a slight draught. When the fire has begun to burn, poke it gently from beneath, and the flame will gradually get through the entire mass of coal, the iron plate beneath gets redbot, and so keeps up a constant combustion, a: the same time dis- persing the heat through the room, instead of its being sent up the chimney, thus entirely consuming the coal, instead of filling the hearth with aehea. When the fire is once made op, 54y about ten o'clock, for the day, an occasional poke, and possibly a single replenishment, suffice for the day. In my own room, where three scuttles were required, one now suffices. LINSEFD LOZENGES, solklified lin.eed tea, laxative and demnleent, flu postage 2d. Kay Bros, Et-ekport, and A 1 Ohemista.

THE STATE OF IRELAND. THE CONSPIRACY TO MURDER OFFICIALS. S'FaRTLING REVELATIONS. Further evidence of a startling and important nature was given at Kilmainham on Saturday. James Brady, Timothy Kelly, Patrick Delaney, and eleven others, were put in the dock, charged with being members of the Conspiracy to Murder Association, and with having murdered Lord Fredk. Cavendish and Mr. Burke. A great sensation was created by Michael Kavanagh, the carman, getting into the witness box. In examination by Mr. Murphy, the Crown prosecutor, Kavanagh deposed that on the '6th of May he' met Joe Brady, Timothy Kelly, and two others at Wrenn's public- house in Dame-street. One of these two he now recognised as Patrick Delaney. He drove them on his car to several places, and ultimately to Phenix Park, near the Gough statue, where they got down and went up the road, telling the witness to wait. Witness saw a cab come past driven by Fitzharris. It stopped some distance up the road. Patrick Delaney sat on a seat near Cie witness, and another man, whom the witness now recognised as James Carey, came up and sat on the seat on the opposite side of the road. Two gentlemen Itesed um in arm. James. Carey and Delaney afterwards jumped on the car, the latter telling the witness to look sharp. The witness drove towards Brady, Kelly, and a number of other men, and on the ray either James Carey or Delaney waved a white handkerchief. They bath got down, and the witness waited near the monument on the car. A cat man, named Neud, drove past when CAIEV and Delaney were on the car, and the witness exchanged I greetings with him. While the witness was waiting two or three tricyclists passed, and one of the riders made an exclamqion. The witness looked round, and saw' the two gen,lemtn who had passed him previouely lying on the road. Brady, Kelly, Delaney, and another men he had driven to the park, came up, and the witness drove rapidly out of the Chapelizod gate towards Terenure. Kelly got off the car at Palmerston Park tramway terminus, and witness drove the others to Lesson Park, where he left them at a public house. The witness also recollected the night of the attack on Mr._Field, the 27th of 'November. Joe Brady en- gaged his cir at the College. He drove to the Quay, and on the way picked up a man whom the witness now tecog- nieed as IS leiel Delaney. He drove them to Hardwicke- street, where he saw Timothy Kelly and Lawrence Hanlon. Brady and Delaney got down, and all four went down the street. They afterwards came back, and all got on the car. Kelly without his hat. The witness drove to a hatter's in Townsend-street, where Kelly got a hat. Thence he drove to a basin near the gasworks, where the witness and Brady took the knives or daggers which had been used and wrapped them in a paper, and witness threw them into the water. After- wards he drove them all to Hatch-street, near the Exhibi- tion Palace, and left them. The witness had driven the same four men whom he drove to the park on May 6th on several previous occasions to the same place. He was pre- viously sworn 39 a member of the society by Timothy Kelly. Tom Doyle was there, and told the witness that Mr. Jas. Mullett and a lot of rich people were in it. He had at different times driven Brady and Kelly to various places. In cross-examination by Dr. Webb, Q.C., who appeared for the prisoners, the witness said he turned informer on Thursday last. In further cross-ex- amination he said he had several times been summoned to the Castle bat he had each time denied any knowl: doge of the affair. The evidence of the carman Noud, who passed Kavanagh, was then taken, and two other wit- nesses then swore to seeing Kavanagh with his car near Wrenn's, in Dame-street, on the 6th of May. Samuel W. Jacob, a youth, who crave evidence at the inquest following the murders, depesed'to seeing a " scuffle " as be was going 'through the park and observing two men fall. He saw four or fire men then .get on a car and drive off, but one of them first ran from one of the prostrate men to the other, and'ap- peered to hit one of them. Two men afterwards passed the bodies as they lay, and turned down Chapelizod-road. Just as the car turned into it,etwo tricyclists came up, and they gave the alarm. The witness was not near enough to recog- nise any of them.

The investigation into the assassination conspiracy case was resumed on Thursday in the Kilmainham Cournuuse. The court was again crowded, notwithstanding that the ut- most discrimination was used as to the admissions. The public interest received a stimulus from the announcement that further evidence would be given by one of the partici- pators in the Phoenix Park murders. The prisoners put forward were James Carey, Timothy Kelley, Joseph Han- lon, Daniel Curley, Michael Fagan, Patrick De- laney, Jatnes Fitzfurris, and Thomas Caffrey. The first witness now ceded was a county Dublin farmer named Cahill, who identified Thomas Ca cry as one of four men (in addition to the driver) who were seated on a car which be saw being driven at a flying pace near the Chapelizod Gate of the Park on the evening of the 6th of May. Mr. Glynn, a builder, spoke to seeing James Carey, whom he knew, seated with another man near the Gough Statue just before two gentlemen, presumably Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke, alighted from a car at the Statue. Thomas Huxley, gardener (an Englishman), identi- fied Timothy Kelly as one of the group of men seen by several persons standing in a clump of trees near the scene of the murders, and Patrick Murray, a labourer, identified Fitzharris as the driver of the cab which was near. William Meagle, brass finisher, one of the two bicyolists who passed close to the spot where the crime was perpetrated, spoke to seeing two separate " tussels" going on. He first identified Michael Fagan as taking part,in one of them, but on that prisoner being brought close to him he said he could net identify him. He declared, however, that Joseph Brady was one of those engaged in the other tussle. After this a police-constable was called to speak to his having on the 12th or 14th June seen Brady and Kelly lurking about the Viceregal grounds. He watched them for a .sort time and they watched him, and then the two prisoners went away. This evidence is supposed to point to a plot against the Lord- Lieutenant. The case was adjourned till to-day, and before the Court rose the magistrate announced that for the, future only the legal geetlemen engaged and the reprters for the press would be atirnittA to this preliminary inquiry. Coun- sel for the prosecution said they hoped to be able to close the case with regard to some of the prisoners to-day, and to ask for a committal for trial.

Lady Ficiretica -13iii-c-SVe in a letter that she reclgthes in Fenianism the honest struggle of a people to attai:a their country's independence. She sympathises with the letters of Feuians repudiating any connection with the Land League, and especially with the assassination conspiracy. She expresses her wish to see Ireland a free and independent kingdom, united with Howland under the same crown. The trial of Mr. Wm. O'Brien, M.P., on a charge of sedi- tious libel, ended on Saturday in a disagreement of the jury, and they were discharged. As soon as the news of the re- sult of the trial reached London, Mr. Parnell despatched the following telegram to the new member for Mallow :—" I congratulate you most heartily upon your virtual acquittal, which is of the utmost importance to the cause of freedom of speech and writing in Ireland." The father of the young man Andrews, who was shot in Dublin about a year ago, has received a letter from the convict Matthew Kinsella, now in Mountjoy Prison, who was sentenced to 20 years' penal servitude for shooting the deceased. At the time it was alleged that Andrews was shot for turning informer, but the convict in his letter to the dead man's father assures him that when examining a revolver-together he gave it a sudden turn by accident, and It went off, shooting the deceased. He carried him down- stairs into the open air, thinking that he would come to, but, finding he was dead, he left his body in the street.

Discontent is the want of self reliance; it is infirmity of will.—R. W. Eelersm. A severe gale raged over the western and northern coasts of these islands :luring Sunday night and Monday morning, and considerable damage was done at the more exposed points. Vess.ls arriving at the southern and Irish ports report very bad weather, and it is feared that the tale of distress will receive many additions.

'The jewellers shop of lqr. Alderman Symons, in the Market Place at Hull, was entered by thieves on Sunday and near midnight a man was seen leaving, who on being searched was found to have a large quantity of valuables in his possession. On an examination being made of the shop a portmanteau was found filled with plunder ready for removal.

On Sunday morning service at the Wesleyan Chapel, Burslem, was brought to an abrupt termination. the preacher had just given out his text when flames were seen to burst forth from the 11 or near the vestry and heating apparatus. The chpi w is speedily cleared. and the fire was isolated by cutting a hole in the floor. Fortunately the damage done was not great.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY. FEBRUARY 17, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY. FEBRUARY 17, 1883.

Mr. James A. Campbell, M.P., who some time since was shot in the eye, has now completely recovered his sight. £lOO reward is offered for the apprehension of the tramp who is supposed to have committed the murder at Small- wood.

OPENING OF PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TITITRDAY. The fourth session of the tenth Parliament of the Queen was opened by Royal Commission at two o'clock this after- the Royal Commissioners being the Lord Chancellor

ment had strenthened their position, it was by a largo sacri- fice of their principles, and he advised them not to jeopar- dise the advantage they had gained at such a cost by foolish endeavours to maintain a reputation for consistency. —Lord HARTINGTON congratulated Sir Stafford iNorthcote upon his restoration to. health, and thanked him for his _ _ .

The Prince of Wales arriv special train at a quarter after eight on Thursday morning, having travelled via Boulogne and Folkestone from Paris in eight hours. The Oxford crew, while practising on Thursday after- noon, smashed their boat in pissing through a lock. The craft was swamped, and a messenger had to be despatched for a fresh boat, in which, when it had arrived, the crew t °Unlined their jnurtieV. James Moore, found- on Tuesday morning in a rooin. in a mill at Stockport with fearful wounds upon him, has died at the Infirmary without being able to give any ati:Ount of the strange occurrence. On Wednesday the young factory opera- tive, Robert Price, who has been arrested on suspicion, was remanded for a week. Foot and mouth disease is epreading to an alarming extent in the Macclesfield district. No fewer than three outbreaks are reported to-day, the contagion having manifested itself at the farms of John Longden, Daniel Ball, and John Booth. An order has been received from the authorities that the March cattle fair must be abandoned in consequence of the oarbreak. Notwithstanding the vigorous action of the authorities, cattle diFease is spreading with alarming rapidity in Scot- land. Four fresh outbreaks were on Thursday reported in Forfarshire' and several new cases occurred in Perthshire, Aberdeenshire, and Midlothian. Pleuro-pneurnonia ap- peared on Thursday in a herd of 30 prime cattle as far north as Ross-shire. The whole of the animals were im- mediately slaughtered.

Their Lordships then adjourned until a quarter to four, when the Lord Chancellor took the oaths and his seat as the Earl of Sel borne, and General Lord Wo'sey also took the oaths and his seat on his elevation to the peerage as Baron lArolsey of Cairo. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four, and formally read the Queen's Speech from ths woolsack. THE QUEEN'S SPEECH. At the close of the last session I had the pleasure of re- cording my gratitude to my sea and land forces for sup- pressing with rapidity and completeness a formidable rebel- lion in Egypt. Since then tranquility has been restored to that 'country. Clemency has been shown by its ruler to the leaders of the rebel- lion, and the withdrawal of the British troops is pro- ceeding as expeditiously as a prudent consideration of the circumstances will admit. The re-constitution of the Go- vernment of Egypt, and the re-organisation of its affairs under the authority of the Khedive have in part been accomplished, and will continue to receive my earnest attention. With regard to the Egyptian question, the time had surely arrived when the Opposition should make up its mind either to challenge the policy of the Govern- ment or prevent the time of the House from being further wasted by desultory criticisms and discussions which could settle nothing. With respect to Ireland, although Secret Societies still existed there, the Government were not only able to bold their operations in check, but had every hope and prospect of being able to trace their operations to their S •urce. The noble, Marquis 'concluded :As to further Irish b-gislation, the right hon. gentleman seemed to think that the Speech contauled some reference to measures which be described as revolutionary and subversive. Ido not admit tint any measures of the Government; even in relation to Ireland, can properly be described as revolu- tionary. (Laughter from the Conservatives.) He only applied those terms to the Land Act, the Arrears Act, and measures of that character; and I can assure the right hon. gentleman that no measures that can be described by him as "revolutionary and subversive" will be presented to the consideration of Parliament in the present session, although it is the intention of my right hon. friend the Chief Secretary to produce several measures of a character which ought not to occupy a great deal of time, but which are measures of considerable importance. div.head: ELOPEMENT FROM EARLESTOWN. CAPTURE OF THE RUNAWAYS.
div.p: ELOPEMENT FROM EARLESTOWN. CAPTURE OF THE RUNAWAYS.

, About two months ago we reported the elopement of a collier named Bolton with the wife of another -collier named .Brown, in whose house near Newton Common Bolton had I.been lodging for a long time past. It will be recollected that both men worked at the Collins Green colliery, but lone morning Bolton complained of being unwell, and . stayed at home. The husband proceeded to his work with- oLt any suspicion of any undue familiarity existing between his wife and Bohan, but when he returned in the afternoon, bah had decamped, and Brown's hard-earned savings, amounting to nearly £3O, had been taken along with a quantity of wearing apparel. Ultimately the police were informed of the occurrence, and a warrant for the apprehension of Bolton was issued. Nothing further was heard of the runaway pair until a few days ago, when information , was received that Bolton, who was then residing with Mrs. Broilm, had been I apprehended at Castle Eden, in Durham. At the Newton Town Hall, on Thursday, before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, James Boltoc, alias Stopforth, was brought up for stealing from the house of Samuel Brown, at Newton Common, on the 11th IDecember last, £27 in money and several articles of wearing apparel. P.S. Commins stated that the prisoner was chargea I under a warrant with stealing the articles specified in the warrant, and the circumstances of the case were briefly , these: Previous and up to the date named the prisoner lodged with the prosecutor, who on that morning went to his work ;i as a collier, leaving the prisoner at home and in bed, the ' latter having stated that he was too LI to go to his work. On the prosecutor returning sometime in the afternoon of the same day, to his great surprise he found that his wife land the prisoner had eloped, and on going upstairs and making an examination of a box in which he had kept some money he found that they had stolen £27, and certain I articles of wearing apparel belonging to the wife had been ' taken away. From enquiries which he made be found that the prisoner and his wife bad gone towards Manchester, and he followed to that city, but afterwards lost all trace of , them. Daring the last week information had reached the ' police that they had made their way to Castle Eden, in Durham, and P.C. Lloyd was dtspatched thereto. That officer received the prisoner into cestody from the police there. He asked that the prisoner might be remanded.—He was accordingly remanded to the Sessions to be held next Saturday.

div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.
ASHTON.

:ADDRESS TO THE MINERS.—The Ashton and Elaydock Miners' Trade Union, at their council meeting, on Saturdiiy, February 3rd, passed a resolution that after their next district meeting all new members should pay 2s ed entrance in all lodges belonging to their district. The following address has been issued :—" The officers and members hereby give all miners a hearty welcome to join before the entrance fee comes into operation, and thus escape the im- post of the same. Fellow-workingmen, why should you not be joined to the association which is established simply to protect your wages, and to endeavour by all legitimate means to elevate the class el which you form a part? Yoa see the necessity for a strong combination every day of your life, ;Ind WO respectfully ask you to consider if it is hot your bounder, duty to do-operate with your fellows to bring this desirable state of things about. What we need in every attempt we make to bring about a better state of things is the sympathy, co-opeption and help of the whole mining community, and if we had this we are fully .per- suaded that in a short time .things would wear quite a diffetent aspect altogether, and your wages would be. higher than what they are. We desire that you will give this question your serious and impartial consideration, and if you do so we are persuaded we shall soon see your zames enrolled on some of our lodge registers.—Trusting you will do so, we are the Officers and Members of the District."

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

SERVICE OF SONG.—A suvice of sacred song was given in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Frodsham, on Wednes- day evening, when the Rev. D. Schofield presided. A selection of readings was given by Mr. W. B. Gibson, of Overton. The choir acquitted themselves very creditably, and the usual vote of thanks to the chairman, Mr. Gibson, and the choir brought the meeting to a close. WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS. The annual meeting in connection with the Wesleyan Home Missions was held in Trinity Chapel, Frodsbam, on Tuesday evening, when Mr. C. E. Taylor, of Wavertree, presided, and addresses were delivered by the chairman, the Rev. Robert W. Hopewell, of London, and Revs. J. M. Bamford and F. F. Edmonds, of Frodshams The collections amounted to £7 7s. 10d. . TEMPERANCE MEETING.—The members of the Rechabite Tent gave another of their interesting entertainments in the Town Hall on Friday evening, when the Rev. D. Schofield presided, and the following took part in the programme, viz. :—J. G. Webb, F. Nickson, John Lloyd, John Beard, W. Lockett, and the choir. An amusing dialogue was given by the following adult members :—Messrs. I'. Nicholas, H. Smith, T. Langwin, H. Aston, W. Sharp, W. Lockett, D. Hooze, and J. Parker.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT.-0a Saturday, John Critchley, an old offender, was brought before Mr. J. Mar- son, at the Occasional Court-house,"Bank-street, and fined 103 and costa for being drunk that morning at Golborne.— James Mills, charged with being drunk at Golborne, with assaulting his wife Jane Mills, and also with stealing wear- ing apparel belonging to his stepson, was remanded to the next Newton Petty Sessions.

GOLBORNE AND DISTRICT LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—The members of the Golborne and District Liberal Association held their annual meeting for the election of officers for the ensuing season, in the Congregational schoolroom, on Mon- day evening last, and a very pleisant gathering was held. There was a goodly number of members with their wives and friends present, and sat down to an excellent tea, which was much enjoyed. The subsequent proceedings were pre- sided over by MT. Roger Yates. The following were elected for the ensuing year :—Mr. W. Mitchell, of Brook Villa, president; Mr. John Unsworth, senior, treasurer; Mr. H. Wright, general secretary; and Mr. W. Eckerslev, financial secretary. A committee of twelve gentremen was also elected. During the evening the statement of accounts for the past year, which wis of a very satisfactory character, and showed a balance of .E 2 138 MI in hand, was read and passed. Hearty votes of thanks were accorded to the re- tiring officers, the waiters, &c., and the meeting was brought to a close by a similar compliment being accorded to the chairman. • A GAME OF CHA.NCE AT GreI.BORNE. At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, Thomas Mitchell, James Roberts, William Riley, and Tianiel Smith, young men, were summoned for playing an unlawful game of chance with dice and coins, on the previous Sunday nighL—ln reply to the charge, Mitchell and Smith stated they were guilty of playing with coins, but not in a public place; and Roberts and Riley pleaded guilty.—P.C. Ratcliffe stated that about half-past eight on the night stated he was on duty with P.C. Whiting, when tkey were directed to a wooden build- ing in a public open yard, in Turton-street. The building was only partly erected, and there was no door to it. They saw the four defendants sitting round a boiled covered with , a numbered cloth, on which coppers were placed. They I watched the defendants play two games, the dice and box being used. A little boy was holding a candle for them.— Superintendent Weir: Is ita place to which be public have a right ?—The witness: Yes, the place is partly erected be- hind some hocses.—The deputy clerk (Mr. White) : How can it be open to the public P—The witness: It is open to the yard, and people can see and go inside it.—The defen- dants were ordered to pay the costs, amounting to Os 6.1 each.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

CAUTION re Ls.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, Arthur Proctor, a lad, was charged with playing at a game called " peggy," at Haydock, on the 25th January.—He was fined ss. including coats. DRUNKENNES AT HAYDOCN.—At the Newton Petty Ses- sions, on Saturday last, Thomas Hall was fined 108. and costs; Wm. Hunt, and Joseph Grove, ss. each and costs for , drunkenness at Haydock. THEFTS AT HAYDOCE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, Henry Gee and Thomas Jackson were charged with stealing eight boards, value 3s the property of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co.—Jackson did not appear, and a warrant far his apprehension was granted.-Gee pleaded guilty.—P.O. Bryan deposed that he saw the two men walking with the boards from the direction of the gasworks towards Old Boston. The boards were 71 feet long, and had been taken from near the gasworks.—The defendant Gee stated that he was not going to steal the boards. He lived under, and worked for the firm, and was raking the boards to make a coal place with.—Mr. Beilby, representing the firm, said Gee was employed by the firm, but had no 1 right to take the boards. They did not wish to unduly press the case. He might have been taking the boards for the purpose he bad named.—The Chairman (Mr. Houghton): You ought to have asked permission,—The defendant : Cer- tainly; I did it without a thought, sir.—He was fined 58 land costs.—Henry Woodyard, 14 years of age, was charged I with stealing 71Ibs. of coal, on the 3rd inst. The defendant was observed coming away from the direction of a heap of coal slack, and had the coal in a basket and bag. He said he did not steal the coals, but some women gave it to him. —He was fined ss, including costs.

div.head: IA- MM.
div.p: IA- MM.

TRESPASS IN PURSUIT OF GAME AT HIGH LEICTI.—Thos. Scott, Joseph Brazendale, and George Brezendale were charged et the Lymm Petty Sessions. yesterday before Messrs. G. C. Dewhurst, Peter Stubs, and H. Stanton, wiih having, on the 11th instant, trespassed in pursuit of game on land occupied by Mr. Frederick Clark, at High Leigh.— The two first-named defendants pleaded guilty, but the latter pleaded not guilty.—George Cook, gamekeeper, said that between half-past ten and eleven o'clock on the morn- ing of the day named he saw the three defendants in a lane adjoining the land. Ho noticed George Brazmdale proceed some distance down the lane and look about, appa- rently to see if there were any persons about. He then went back to where the other two defendants were stand- ing, and witness saw two of the defendants, .-:.cett and Js. Brazendale, enter the field and spread a net, and then pro- ceed down the field.—Sergeant Foden seid that from infor- mation be received he went in the direction of the place, and met the defendants, and found upon them ti,e net pro- dueed.—The defendants expressed their sorrow for having committed the offence, and promised that it eleould not occur again.—The Bench said that as there was nothing re- corded against the defendants previously, they were inclined to deal very leniently with them, and a doe of only lOs and costs each would be imposed. ZIOIsT INDEPENDENT METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, CURREY- LANE, Lvmer.—The annual tea party in connection with the above school took place on Monday last, when *lOO persons sat down. The tables were presided over by the follow- ing ladies :—Mrs. H. Moston, Mrs. Thornicroft, Mrs. G. golf., Mrs. Cooke, and Miss Thornicroft. After tea a public meeting was held, when Mr. James Mort occupied the chair, addresses being delivered by Messrs. J. Loxley (of Warring- ton) and T. Collier (of Lowton Common). Recitations were given in a highly creditable manner by the scholars. H. Daniels caused roars of laughter and loud applause during the reciting of" Eawr folk -and th' owd bellmoc." A dialogue entitled "The diecontented mare was given in excellent style by the following :—Mr. Flurry (the discon- tented man), Richard Hewitt ; Mildman (au assistant), David Daniels; Mrs. Hurry, Miss C. Thornicroft; Susan (maid). Miss E. Holt ; John (the man servant), T. Knowles; Joe Lightheart (a peckmau), 11. Daniels. '1 he choir, under the able leadership of Mr. A. Ellison sung the anthems "The Sunday school army " and "Awake, awake Jerusalem, 'my glorious home." in a manner that cannot be too highly spoken of. The meeting was brought to a close about 9-30 by the singing of the doxology. Thus ended one of the best tea meetings ever held in connection with the above place. On Tuesday the scholars were provided with an ex- cellent tea, which WAS free. After .tea several innocent games took place in the schoolroom, until shortly after nine o'clock, when each scholar received an orange. The meet- ing terminated by the singing of the doxology. NANTIVICH.

Colonel the Hon. Thomas Grenville Cholmonda ley died at Abbots Moss, Nantwich, at the end of last week. e deceased was the second son of Thomas, first Lord Dela- mere, by Henrietta Elizibeth, fourth daughter of the late Sir Watkin Williams Wynn, Bart., and was born 4th Augnet' 181 S. He was educated at Rugby, and afterwards entered the army as ensign in 43rd Foot, of which regimtr t he be- came captain in 1843. For many years he Was Lieutenant Colonel of the Ist Royal Cheshire Militia, and was Lieut.- Colonel of the 3rd battalion of the Cheshire Regiment. The late Colonel married in August, 1850, Katharine Lucy second daughter of tLe late Sir Tattoo Sykes, Bart., by whom he leaves numerous issue. ATTEMPTED LOVE SIJICIDE.—At Nantwich Police Court, on Monday afternoon, Annie Bradshaw, a young lady, was charged with attempting to poison herself. The act was perpetrated at Piggott's Crown Hotel, Nan twich, where the prisoner had taken apartments, having run away horn her borne in consequence of a quarrel between herself and her lover.—Mr. Brooke, so! icitor, who prosecuted, said Mr. Piggott, who took the laudanum and chlarafortn from the prisoner, was unable to be present. He (Mr. Brooke) had

received/an extraordinary communication from Miss Brad. shaw,in which she said a good many things. It was necessary Mr. Piggott s'lould be present,-as he would depose that pri. soner put poison in some brandy and water, and it was onls.; -taken from- her after a struggle.—Sergeant Lewis then deposed that from information received he went to the Crown Hotel, where he was told prisoner had attempted to poison herself. Ho was also informed that she had written to.a young man named Shore declaring that he was the cause of her death. ,He had her watched.—Mr. Brooke said there was enough poison in her possession to kill two people.—Sergeant Lewis said prisoner confessed to being so miserable that she intended to kill herself. Prisoner was then remanded.—The prisoner was again brought utifen Wednesday, and the magistrate ordered her be discharged on enterieg upon her own recognisance to come up attain when called on, the meant of bail beiiag fixed at L5O.

ITPHOLLAND. A *VOLUM LADY SUING HER SoLICITOII.—At the Liver- pool Chancery Court, on Tuesday, ,before Vice-Chancellor Bristow, judgment was given in the ease of Naylor V. Wood. This was an action brought by Miss Martha Naylor, of Upholland, near Wigan, again et Frederick Wood, solidi- ter, to set aside the elle of the reversionary interest of err& eigth share in the estate of her aunt, Mrs. Jane Atherton. She also &aught to se; aside certain bills of costs charged against her by the defendant in 1879 and at other times. It appears that the plaintiff, who was a ward in Chancery, contemplated marriage, and the defendant acted for her in getting the consent of the court to the wedding, which, however, was broken Off. He also acted for her when she came of age in getting a legacy out of court, her aunt hav- ing previously died. Several borrowing transaztions took p,ace between them, and .when a settlement came to be effected certain bills of costs were deducted.--.-His Honour, in delivering judgment, said he would set aside the deed of assignment on the ground that the defendant at the time of the purchase was still in the position of solicitor to his client, and did not exercise sufficient care in acquainting her with the value of the property. He also found that the estate was worth £lOO more than the defendant had given for it; and, in additien to setting aside the deed of assign- ment, be directed the taxation of costs and disallowed certain items of compound interest. At the same time, he wished it to be understood that there was no imputatiou of "mural fraud" against the defendant, for all the latter bad done was to act in a careless manner. WIGAN. ACCIDENTS IN COLLIERIES.—At an inquest at Marsh Green Wigan, on Tuesday morning, on a man killed by a fall oicoal at the Offen Coal and Cannel C.mpany's pit, Mr. Hall, Government inspector of mines, said that during the year about 20 persons were killed from falls of coal, not falls of roof. He was satisfied that many of these accidents might be prevented if men and managers would take a little more care and pains to prop the coal. This accident might easily have been prevented. INSFORD.

SUBSIDENCE.—The general subsidence of the district con- tinues to attract attention. Now it is a door of a room that will not shut, or a window that will not rise, here a water main is twisted so that the street is like a river, or a gas main is pulled out of joint, and if in some firm clayey part it may be for months a channel for most part of the gas to pass along. The water and gas pipes are constantly break- ing at Winsford. One of the former on Saturday night made a river in High-street, the detriment being most felt by those. who had the water cut off for a time. MISSIONARY SERVICES. The annual mission services were conducted at Winsford in connection with the. Prime-

tive Methodists at both High-street chapel and StatiOn-road, on Sunday. Sermons were preached by the Rev. J. QaarmbY and the Rev. T. Turner, the one the deputation, the other the circuit superintendent. The congregations at both were good. The public meetings were held on Tuesday evening, atStation-road, when the above speakers were supplemented by Messrs. T. Gibson and W. G. Newall, and on Wednesday by the Rev. J. T. Maxwell, who supported Mr. John Stubbs, the chairman, and advocated the cause very well.
