FATAL ACCIDENT AT CHESTER. -- A Bar KILLED AND THREE INURED.—An accident of a distressing character occurred at Handbridge, an outskirt of the city of Chester, shortly after one o'clock on Thursday. It appears that off Greenway-street a bye-road runs, and that on Thursday four little children were together under a wall, witching; the, movements of a frog, when the wall fell upon them, two of the children being buried in the de/is. The two others^ escaped with but slight injuries. Charles Birch, six years of age, was extricated dead.

CELE:SIIIRE DAIRY FARMERS' A SSOCIATION.—A meeting of the Cheshire Dairy Farmers' Association was held on Saturday at Chester. Mr. H. J. Tollemache,. M.P., presiding when the special committee appointed some time ago for the purpose of drawing up a statement of the objects of the asso- ciation, revising the rules, and considering the amount of the remuneration to be given to Mr. R. L. Wright, the late secretary, presented a report, which it was decided to sub- mit fer approval to a full general meeting to be lield earl* next month. It was resolved to apnoint a secretary at £4O per annum; and that the sum of .£2O be paid to Mr. Wright, the late gecretary, for his services in connection with the Association.

Before Lord SALISBURY Sa.ys 1.4) enlighten an audience on

Irish affairs we hope he will make himself better acqainted with the statistics of Irish crime, and treat his hearers to a little more of fact and less of fiction. We have heard a great deal from time to time from the Con- servatives, and also from the Home Rulers, as to the Arrears Act being a failure, but it would seem there is no justification for such a conclusion. It was thought the tenants could not avail themselves of the provisions of the Act because they were overburdened with- arrears, yet the CHIEF SECRETARY assures us that nearly flinty thousand are participating in its benefits, several thousand more than was at one time anticipated would be the case. To use the words of Mr. TREVELYAN "the tenant's title to his holding is now as good as the landlord's title to his estate," and we believe with him it is only necessary that the tenants should be left to pursue their avocations in peace in order to ensure a period of prosperity provided, of course, there are fairly good har- vests—such as has been unknown in the country. Unfortunately. however, in Ireland there is a class of men who live by agitation, and who will not leave the tenant farmers alone. These are the men who would have us believe that the Government are using their repressive measures NI order that the rich may live at ease, and that the English connection may be preserved. The facts falsify such an assertion. It is the humble, the poor, and the unpro- tected who have profited, .and that to a much greater extent than the wealthy. On the whole, the CHIEF SECRETARY'S review of what has been done and what yet remains to be done is a hopeful one, and gives ground for the belief that the progress towards the, restoration of law and order will be gradual, and at the same time sure. We trust, however, that no one will be foolish enough to suppose that because during the past two or three years we have done so much for Ireland, we have done enough. As Mr. H. GLADSTONE pointed out the other evening, a country with over five millions of a population must constantly require more or less attention at our hands; it is because in previous years we have treated Ireland with but scant justice that we have had so much trouble in that country recently. Let it be ours to make the Irish people feel that however they may have been looked upon in the past they are now one with us in every sense; make each and all conscious that they have a voice in the good government of the country; let them enjoy all the political advantages which we in England possess, then there need be no fear but that the future of Ireland will be brighter than it has been in the past.

THE demonstration of Widnes Liberals on Tuesday even- ing last showed that the leaders of the party of progress in the town retain their vitality and vigour, and the indi- vidual members of the Association their enthusiasm, a fact which is in marked contrast to the apathy exhibited by their opponents, Who, if we may accept their few public appearances as an indication, love darkness rather than light. The record of the work accomplished during the past year was a very, gratifying one. Minor matters of detail connected with organisation had received every attention, whilst a signal success had been achieved in the important work of registration, and the chairman did not forget to pay a fitting tribute of praise to the gentlemen who had been the chief means of its accomplishment—Mr. E. Carey, the painstaking vice- president, and the energetic and able secretary, Mr. 11. B. Shores. The party at the last revision made a nett gain of 123 votes over their Conservative opponents, exclusive of 58 re-claims. Mr. F. K. Muspratt, the president, delivered, in moving the adoption of the report, a speech characterised by a thorough acquaintance with political affairs, and a knowledge of the principles which guided them. In a few graphic and telling phrases, he defended the action of the Government in Egypt, eulogised their administration of the war, and reviewed the prospective legislation of the present session. County Government, the anomalies of land tenure, the extension of the county franchise, were referred to. The opinions expressed by Mr. Forwood in the Contemporary Review on the subject of county franchise, were ridiculed in a quiet but effective way, and that gentleman was also made the subject, at the hands of Mr. Bosomworth, of a couplet, which was scathing in its apt application. Mr. Muspratt is of opinion that a measure for the extension of the Borough Franchise to the counties cannot be much longer delayed, and we hold the same view. The time is not far distant when thousands of workingmen in Widnee, who are able and willing to vote upon political principles, will have granted to them that power, and in the redistribution of seats by which it will be accompanied, en- immediately followed, the claims of Widnes and the surrounding hamlets, will, we doubt not, be recognised. The broad hut just principles enunciate by Mr. Muspratt on the English Land Question are such as will be willingly accepted by every true and honest Libera . For a complete settlement of the land question, which has rapidly matured owing to the recent legislation for Ireland, he contended that two things were necessary. Firstly, that trade in land should be freed from all the absurd restrictions with which it is at present burdened; and secondly, that the tiller of the soil should have absolute security for his improvements, and for the capital he has expended in the cultivation of the soil. These principles are in perfect accord with the views expressed by Mr. H. Broad- hurst, Mr. Jessie Collings, and other land re- formers, and when adopted and carried out by our statesmen, we may expect to see a prosperous peasantry, a successful agriculture, and a wealthier nation. In the present calmness of the political atmosphere, the deplorable state of Ireland attracts the attention of politi- cians in a high degree, and the speeches that followed were to a great extent devoted to the affairs of that unhappy country. It is a subject of deep interest to the population of Widnes, a third of which consists, it is calculated, of people of Irish nationality, and we would advise our readers to peruse the speeches of Mr. E. R. Russell, Mr. S. Little, i and Mr. Joseph Morrison, which are reported elsewhere. In concluding we would congratulate the Liberals of Widnes on the efficiency of their organisation, and we trust, and believe, that the success attained last year will be transcended in this and future years.

" cratur " by impulsive Hibernian' has a tendency to sink—in a metaphorical sense, of course—a :man's head beneath the waters, but it has been vouchsafed to these later times, and to the district of Parr, near St. Helens, to raise up a man who is prepared to maintain that whiskey has the power to keep a man above wator. At an inquest at Parr the other day on the body of a an who was drowned, a philoso- phical juryman oracularly stated that it was I scarcely possible for a man to sink if he were full of whiskey. Unfortunately, as has been the case on the , first enunciation of all great truths, this revelation was received with nothing but mirth and incredulity, otherwise the matter Might have been laid before , the public more in &rims*. However, more scepticism I never yet disproved a great scientifiJ truth, and it may be that the propounder of this truth—if truth it should prove to be—has, like many of those who have made similar discoveries, proved its correctness beyond the possibility of denial, by many and fre- quent personal experiments. If so, whiskey has a great future before it. It will be more than ever true of it that it makes a man " o'er a' the ills o' life victorious."

It would seem there are some curious paupers in the Conway Union. A recant meeting of the Guardians disclosed the fact that a pauper at Colwyn Bay had sent a telegram to the Board to the effect that she could not enter the workhouse on a particular day because she was unprovided with a pair of boots, which caused the rev, chairman who presided to in- quire whether she wanted a carriage and pair to fetch her. And it is not at all unlikely that she may have done so, for it was a shilling she had received from the relieving officer which paid for the telegram, and a very little more woul4 have been sufficient to pro- vide the equipage. It also transpired at the same meetine• that another pauper in the house, when he wanted' anything being done for him by the Master, and went for that important functionary, always took a poker in his hand the better to enforce his de- I mands. It will strike most people that the governor's place cannot be quite a bed of roses; also, that money is more plentiful than it ought to be when it can be used by the paupers in telegraphing. Mr. A. Arnold, one of the Liberal members for Salford, delivered a most interesting address to his constituents on Monday evening. The hon. memb-r is an authority on all questions appertaining to the extension of the franchise, as well as on all matters in which land is concerned, and to his utterances•on these subjects, therefore, considerable importance is attached. Mr. Arnold predicts that when the two great political parties cone to close quarters on the extension of the franchise the great battle will be fought over the retention of the property vote. The Tories will fight for the principle that a man who has money shalt be able to buy a vote for every consti- tuency; while the Liberals will be in fay.ntr of the abolition of that franchise. Plural voting is, of course, an injustic., it is eontrary to the letter and spirit of the Act of Henry VI., whi ;II provided that members should be chosen in every county "by people dwelling and resident therein "—not by absente3s,but if there is to be plural voting at all, Mr. Arnold suggests the form to which least objection oould be taken, and that is by giving each member a Tote for,nay every 1,000 or 5,000 electors who gave him their suffrages. The suggestion is a very good one, and as Mr. Arnold says himself, it is about the i only one which possesses a show of equity for plural I voting. The excellent lecture on Ireland which Mr. H. Gladstone delivered in Leeds the other night has excited the hypercriticism of the Baron de Worms, who has been endeavouring—but I think he has failed—to make political capital out of it. Mr. Glad- stone said the history of the English Government in Ireland was a complete catalogue of political blunders and he added that before, a comparatively recent period probably no country in the world had seen less of peace and more of misery. Mr. Gladstone, how- ever did not blame any particular party for this, for he distinctly said that from the responsibility of most of this no Government in England was exempt. Notwithstanding this explicit statement, the member for Greenwich, in an after-dinner speech at Man- chester, charged Mr. Gladstone that he blamed the Tories for all our trouble in Ireland, a thing which probably he would never dream of doing. At the same time, we air know that the coercive policy in Ireland of the late Government—when the country was comparatively tranquil—has been the cause of mach of the mischief we have experienced-there; and the Conservative party has indeed very little cause for congratulation on that score. Baron de Worms ought really to be more accurate in his criticisms; without accuracy, in fact, they can possess neither point nor force.

ITilt PARCELS PosT.—We understand that the Post Office authorities have been in communication with the Lords of the Treasury, and that it is now definitely arranged that the Inew parcels post will come into operation on the let of June *ext.

SPECIAL SERMONS AT BETHESDA CHAPEL, RUNCORN.— The Rev. Professor A. Halliday, principal at the Methodist Free Church College, Manchester, preached to good congrega- tions at Bethesda Congregational Chapel, on Sunday morn- ing and evening. His discourses were listened to with marked attention, and collections were made in aid of thoa horn. missions.

THE BEGGING NUISANCE AT Rumconw.—On Monday, at Runcorn Pejtv Sessions, Thomas Noon was charged with begging in Blantyre-street, on Friday night, and, on the evidence of P.C. Burkhill and P.S. McMichael, he was sent to gaol for 14 days' hard labour.—A similar sentence was passed upon Thomas Jones for begging in Regent-street, on Saturday night.—P.S. McMichael proved the case. A WIDNES SALVATIONIST AT REsr.—On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, William Leather, who some time ago was a member of the Salvation Army, was charged with sleeping in Gasket!, Deacon, and Co.'s chemical works on the previous night without any visible means of snb- sistence.—P.C. Skinner, who described the prisoner as a scamping fellow, proved the case and Mr. Brock committed him to gaol for seven days' hard

WIDNES DIWNEARDS.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, John Byron was fined 7s 6d and costs for being drunk and disorderly; for similar offence Martin Grady was tined 51 and costs, John Loftus 5s and costs, John Harrison 5s and noes, Ann Walsh 5s and costs, John Taylor 5s and costs. Thomas Green 5s and costs. Martin Mannion was tined lOs and costs for being drunk whilst in cbarc,e of a horse and cart in Waterloo-road on the Ist inst. Defendant said he had been driving a wedding party, and had had three glasses of drink.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WO.—On Wednesday, at Widnes P,t!ty Session, Mr. G. H. Danby, clerk to Widnes School Mord, prosecuted the following parsons, who were each tined 5s for committing a breach of the Education Act:—Thomas Coffey, Thomas Brown, Dennis Keogh, John Flood, Pat Quinn, Margaret Traynor, Eli; abeth Williamson, Thomas Welsh, Francis Garbutt, Wil I ism Crinnon, Frederick Gilbert, Mary A. Bowyer, Thomas Frann, Martha Holden, Edward Pardoe, Patrick Keelcy, Peter McCafferty, John Keating. LIQUIDATION.—The first statutory meeting of the credi- tors of William Howard, of Church-street, St. Helens Ann Street West and Waterloo-road, Widnes, wholesale grocer arid provision dealer, was held on Thursday, at Messrs. J. B. and B. Leach, solicitors, Whiteehapel, Liverpool. The statement presented showed liabilities, £2,709; assets (less preferential claims), £1,494. A composition of lOs in the pound was accepted, payable by four equal instalments, at three, six, nine, and twelve months, Mr. J. B. Leach being appointed trustees to distribute the composition. The principal creditors were represented by Mr. G. H. Russell, secretary of the Creditors' Association, Withy-grove, Man- chester; Messrs. RoAse, Price, and Co., North John-street, Liverpool ; and Mr. J. Balenar, North-street, Liverpool. The debtor was represented by Messrs. Swift and Son, solicitors, St. Helens.

A Row BETWEEN WOMEN AT WIDNES. A married woman named Ellen Twigg was charged at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, with assaulting Maly Ann Bur- bridge. On the 3rd February, it seemed, from the evidence of the complainant and witnesses, that the formerwas pass- ing the defendant's house. The defendant "called on" complainant, who, on going up to her, was informed that " Jem wasn't come home yet." "I don't want your husband when he does come home," was the reply. "All that rwan to ask is that you will pay what you owe me." The de- fendant then made use of bad expressions, and saying, "1 will give it you," knocked the complainant to the ground. This was twice repeated, and then defendant seized her by the hair, large quantities of which she pulled from the com- plainant's head.—Defendant alleged that the complainant was drunk at the time, and was the assailant, but the Bench were of a different opinion, and fined her 103 and costs. WORKING MEN'S MISSION MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT BO- CIETY.—At the meeting of this society, which was held last Saturday evening, Mr. D. Hill read a very able essay on "The responsibility of parents." The essayist spoke of the parents being responsible for the proper training of the children who were placed under their care, and referred to how they were to be brought up—by teaching them the simple prayer of childhood, by taking them to the House of God, not to send them, go themselves, and show their chil- dren the example; also by teaching them daily the Word of God, the precious trutle which would guide them in years to corns. The essayist also spoke of the number that are sunk in sin and degradation through the neglect of their parents in their young days. At the close, the essayist was complimented for the able manner his essay was got up, and it was hoped he would read another at some future meeting en "The duty of children to their parents." After a slight debate the meeting was closed by singing the Doxology. BURGLARY AT WARRINGTON.—On Sunday evening an entrance was effected to the premises of Mrs. Mellor, grocer, Horsemarket-street, whilst the family were at chapel. On the return of the family, about 20 minutes to eight o'clock, it was discovered that the shop had been entered, and that a few shillings in copper had been taken from the till. On proceeding upstairs it was found that all the drawers had been ransacked, and some valuable gold and silver articles abstracted. These consisted of a gentleman's gold centre seconds watch, open face, white dial, m titer, Glover,Cronton, number not known, name "Fame Mellor" engraved on dome; a lady's long gold chain, small cable pattern; a lady's silver locket, large size, engraved on one side, and diagonal cut, with male photograph in each side without glass covers; a lady's silver necklet, secret link pattern, which forms a square in chain, very thick and strong, broken in one place, and pieced with silver wire; and a gold Albert curb pattern with seal attached. Other valuable articles were left on a chair and dresser. The burglars obtained admittance to the premises through the shop, and must have been familiar with the habits of the family. A reward of £2 has been offered for such information as will lead to the recovery of the pro- perty and the apprehension of the thief.

TRICKS OF RAILWAY TRAVELLING: A CAPTURE AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. Holbrook Craskell, senior, and Mr. John Brock, George Atherton was summoned on a charge of attempting to de- fraud the London and North-Western Railway Company.— Mr. Ferrand appeared for the prosecution, and the defendant, who did not appear, was represented by his wife. From Mr. Ferrand's statement, which was borne out by the evid- ence of Josepn Hardy, pointsman, Mr. Smith, stationmaster, and P.C. Brown, it appeared that the defendant, who was in the habit of coming to Widnes to visit his friends almost weekly, and on the 13th January he took a return ticket from Edge Hill to Garston, for which he paid 101. A re- turn ticket to Widnes would have cost 2s. The defendant entered the train, from which he was seen to alight on its arrival at Widnes. He gazed about him as if to discover if he was watched by any person, and then he left the station by the slope down which luggage is conveyed. His tactics had, however, been observed by the pointsman, who called the attention of the porter to his tnovenvnts. The porter ran down the steps, and around to the bottom of the slope where he met the defend int, and conveyed him into the presence of Mr. Smith, the stationmaster. He then produced a return ticket from Edge Hill to Gatston, and !informed Mr. Smith that he resided in Pecloniff-street. It was discovered that this was it false address, the defendant living in Micawber- street. He admitted the offence when the summons was served, and Mr. Ferrand, as this conduct was of frequent oc- currence, and had, he believed, been followed by the defen- dant each week, asked their worships to inflict the full penalty, 40s and costs.—The evidence having been heard, the Bench mulcteg the defendant in the sum of £2, and costs 15s.

DBFRAPDING THE LONDON AND NORTII-WESTERK RAILWAY COMPANY ON RUNCORN BRIDGE—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. William Bankes and Mr. -Charles Reynolds, James Bennett was summoned on a charge of having, on the 17th January, fraudulently passed along the Runcorn Bridge, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company, without having paid the tolls payable for so doing.—Mr. Preston (accompanied by Mr. ',errand) appeared for the company, and Mr. F. A. Lake- defended —The defendant,pleaded guilty, and Mr. Preston related the facts of the case. He pointed out that the com- pany had power to charge ?A. for every passenger who, crommed the bridge' but as a concession to workmen and others they issued weekly tickets, which were generally issued on Tuesdays. These tickets were of different colours, and one colour was used on each eighth week. Each ticket was nipped twice, once on the Tuesday and once on the Wednesday, and it therefore followed that the person who held it was the only person who was entitled to it. In this case Helpin, the collector, was on duty, and having been a servant of the company there for some time, be was well acquainted with the passengers and the weekly ticket holders. 'On the evening of the day in question, Ifelpin had his suspicions aroused that the defendant had no ticket, and when the latter came up the steps with several others who held proper tickets, he asked the defendant to produce his. The defendant showed a ticket but refused to allow the collector to examine it, and sooner than do so tore it up before his face. He then threw it away and rushed past the collector. Ilelpin took up the ticket, which he found bore the date 21st August . last, and that the defendant had really and truly, and in a bare-faced manner, defrauded the eompany by crossing. The defendant, how- ever, was well known, and these proceedings were taken not with a view of inflicting a heavy fine upon a single in- dividual, but to let the public know that conduct of this ' kind was not a 11,-k—that it meant punishment. Although the amount might only be twopence or threepence yet as frequent attempts were made to avoid the payment of that sum, it was a duty the company owed to the shareholders to endeavour, as far as they could, to put a stop to this fraudulent system. If the case were proved, he asked the Bench to deal with the defendant as they thought best, aria p,inted out that the penalty was not exceeding 40s.— Mr. Lake said ht Lafl advised the defendant to plead guilty because there was no act-ht that he had techni- cally committed the offence with which he was charged, although he thought their worships would see that there was little criminality in it. The defendant had been a con- tract ticket holder for some months, and on this occasion he was on night shift at Widnes, where he worked. He, how- ever, forgot to take with him a shilling with which to pur- chase his contract, but thinking he could borrow that amount from a fellow workman he did not return home. Unfortunately for him he was unable to borrow the money. He, however, had to get to Widnes, and finding the old ticket in his pocket he made use of it in order to pass the collector. It Was a very foolish and wrong thing to do, but not an offence which he thought their worships would , visit with a heavy nenalty.—The Bench fined the deleavizt 20s. and costs 9s. 6cl,
CHANGE RINGING AT FARNWOIZTH PARISH CHURCH.-.

On Saturday evening six ringers of tbe.above church rang a true peal of 720 changes grandsire moor, in good style, in 201 minutes. The ringers were :--1.5t, A. Whitfield ; 2nd, P. Cave; 3rd, J. Large; 4th, J. T. Lowe; sth, T. Fletcher ; 6th. J. Latchford, junior. Jr. J. Large conducted.

MYSTERIOUS DEATII OF A RUNCORN YOUTIL—To-day (Saturday) an inquest Will be held on the body of Jana Os Briscoe, 15 years of age, the stepson of Mr. Thomas Lydiate, grocer, Devonshire-square, Runcorn. The youth, who had been ill for about eight days, died an Thursday morning, under such circumstances that Dr. Carruthers' who had attended him, would not certify as to the cause ofdeat h. The coroner directed a post mortem examination to be made, and we understand the result goes to show that the cause of death was inflammation of the brain. It is supposed that the deceased received a blow whilst playing football at War- rington about a fortnight ago. ST. 111ARY'&, WIDNES.—A mission of most remarkable success has been brought to:a close at St. Mary's, Widnes. It lasted three weeks and two days, and was conducted by the Rev. Fathers McLoughlin, Morgan, Bradshaw, Geoghegan, and Urhany, Redemptorists from Bishop. Eton. The crowds attending the services were such that aimost from the outset the large schools of St: Patrick as well as the church were filled by seven o'clock every evening. And such was the enthusiasm of the people' that the confes- sionals were surrounded by eager crowds the whole day long. Although only workingtnen were heard after the evening service, yet many of them had to wait several nights till after eleven o'clock before they could succeed in making their confession. Over four thousand persons approached the sacraments on the occasion of the mission. A large number of Protestants attended the services, upwards of forty being received into the church. Several others are to be received shortly.

LANCASITIRE AND YORNSHIRE RAILWAY.-1D their report for the last half-year, the directors of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway state that while the gross receipts were £27,000 in excess of the corresponding half of 1881, the working expenses have increased £78,000, the result being a dividend per cent. less, or a reduction of * per cent. for the whole year. The diminution of dividend is attributed to the heavy repairs to works and stock, the continued diminution of the receipts from passenger traffic in proportion to the number of passengers carried, the decrease in the receipts from the more profitable description of goods carried, and also—" to some extent "—the cost occasioned by the severe snowstorm, which cost the Sheffield Company, it will be re- membered, £lO,OOO. Tbe directors are promoting a bill for the construction of a railway 12i miles long between Pendleton and Hindley to relieve the crowded traffic be- tween Manchester and Bolton, and for other purposes, the total amount of share capital to be raised tinder the powers of the bill beingnearlv two millions. Mr. Thomas Barnes is retiring from the office of chairman on account of the state of his health.

k RUNCORN SEAMAN'S LARK. - At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Captain Hazlehurst, Richard Williams, who was dressed in the garb of a seaman, was charged with having on the previous day stolen three blan- kets, one quilt, and a large quantity of other articles, the property of a mariner named Evan Morgan. The prosecutor is the ctretaker of the brigantine "Clara Novello," at pre- sent lying in Runcorn Docks. He was conveying the articles produced, which were his property, to the office of Mr. Marwood, ship broker, Top Locks, when he met the pri- soner, who asked to be allowed to carry the bag to the station. The prosecutor replied that he was not in want of his services, and entered the office, leaving the bag outside on the steps. He found, on returning after a few minutes' absence, that the bag had been removed. About half- past three the same day Annie Guy, living at the shop of Mr. Booth, butcher, Percival's-lane, saw the prisoner ptss along with the bag upon his back, and Eliza- beth Jqbnson, domestic servant, Mariners' Hotel, deposed that the prisoner left the bag in the bar-room of the hotel. Subsequently' P.S. McMichael apprehended the prisoner whilst offering a pair of trousers for sale to Roger /Looney, second-hand clothes dealer, Regent-street. The prisoner protested that he had only "done it for a lark on the old man," but as he had only just been released from gaol, he was committed to the Knutsford Sessions for trial.

ALLEGED ASSATJLT ON A MOTHER.—Thomas Gayter, rough looking young fellow, was summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a charge of having, on the 4th inst., assaulted Susannah Gtyter, his mother. From the evidence of the mother and her son Joseph, aged 17, it appeared that on the Sunday in question, at noon, the de- fendant and the latter were fighting outside the house. Dur- ing the struggling the defendant smashed the window with his back, and the mother on going outside found that the defendant bad hold of his brother by the neck. He was using such force that his brother's face became black, and froth fell from his mouth. The mother screamed that her son was being killed, and the defendant's wife and another woman went to quell the strife. Defendant, however, k;cked them, and in reply to his mother's entreaties to desist, he said, ' I'll kill the —." She then screamed for "police," when he turned upon her and said," ou old —, if you don't go away, I'll hit you." He followed his threat up by striking her over the mouth with his clenched hand, and also on the right side of the face near the ear. She fainted away, and remembered nothing further of the disturbance. In consequence of his conduct she had not spoken to him for twelve months.— Defendant alleged that his brother was "always agate" of him, and his father advistA him to take no notice, hut on the Sunday in question he could stand it no longer. He denied striking his mother, and asked that the case should be ad- journed in order that be could produce witnesses.—The case was adjourned for a fortnight.

ALLEGED BREACH OF THE LICENSING ACT BY N WIDNES PCDLICAN.—At Whines Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. F. S. Gossage and Mr. John Brock, James Tilly, landlord of the Norton Arms Hotel, Widnes, was summoned .to answer a charge of permitting drunkenness on his licensed premises.—Mr. Bartlett, of Liverpool,.apprared for the defendant.—From the evidence of P.C.'s Brown and Almond it seemed that on the 2nd inst. these officers 'visited the defendant's house. In the taproom they fonnd four men, one of whom was a man named Martin Griffin. Griffin. who was very drunk, was sitting at a table with a glass of whiskey, three-pea-VI full, before him, out of which he was seen to drink. Mrs. Tilley, who was present, observed that she had not noticed his state before, and denied that he had been served with drink. Turnint, to the servant she exclaimed," Dear me, do you see what a state this man is in ?" while Griffin stated "This whiskey is mine. I paid 3 I for it." Another man said the spirits belonged to a man fro re Farnworth. By Superintendent Barker Griffin was afterwards taken into custody.—Mr. Bartlett called the defendant, who stated he did not, and no one else could have, served him. Ha would not swear, however, that he had not been -served by anyone else.—John Hague, labourer, Oxford-street, deposed that he was in the bar on he night in question, and he positively stated Griffin was not served with whiskey. A young man in the room said he could not drink his whiskey, and Griffin reached over the table, lifted the glass to his lips, and drank the con- tents.—Mrs. Tilley having given evidence, the Chairman (Mr. Gossage) said he considered the police perfectly right in having the case investigated, but the offence Was net suite brought home to the defendant, and the case would be dismissed.

ALLEGED ROBBERY OF A WATCTI AT WEATON.—Before Mr. W. Bankes, at Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, Mary Ann Fishwick, a domestic servant, was charged in custody with having, on or about the 12th September last, stolen a watch, the property of Samuel B mow, landlord of the ,Royal Oak, Weston. From the evidence it appeared that prior to the end of last Sept. the prisoner was a domestic servant in the employ of the prosecutor. During her resi- dence in the house a watch, which was usually kept in an unlocked box in a bedroom, was missed, and until Monday. the 12th inst., no trace of its whereabouts -was discovered. On that day, however, a plumber, named Samuel Jones, who lived with the prosecutor, went to the house of the prisoner's sister,. Mrs. Lloyd. The latter then handed him the long-lost watch, and explained that it came into her possession through the prisoner. One morn- ing in September the prisoner, whilst in the service of the prosecutor, asked Mrs. Lloyd to ietch a watch which was. being repaired for her at Mr. Carr's. She stated that she had purchased- it at a pawnshop, paying for it in weekly instalments. Mrs. Lloyd obtained the watch after paying for the repairs, hut refused to give it to her sister, the prisoner. Mr. T. S. Carr, watchmaker, deposed that the watch was repaired by him for a yirl of the name of Fish- wick. When apprehended. by P.C. Cooper, the prisoner alleged' she had never seen the watch, and' knew nothing whatever about it. She was committed to Knutsford, Sessions for trial, the Bench consenting to admit her to bail herself in £lO and two sureties of £2O each.

Tina ATLAS CICEIVICAL COMPANY, LIVITED. The eighth ordinary generalmeeting of the above company was held in the large room of the Central Hotel, on Tuesday last, at Et-30 o'clock, under the presidency of Joseph Cook, Esq., ex-Mayor of St. Helens the chairman of the company. The minutes of the last meeting having been read and COP., firmed, the Chairman laid the directors report and balance skeet before the meeting. He thought the company might be congratulated on the result of the year's working, for although the chemical trade had been more depressed than ever, and lower prices had ruled in the market than had- prevailed before, the amount of profit realised had exceeded that of last year by about .0,200. The directors recom- mended that out of the net profits £2;000 should be placed to the credit of the depreciation fund, which would then stand at £lO,OOO, and the balance carried forward to next year's account. He concluded by moving the adoption of the report and balance sheet as presented.—The motion was seconded by Peter Bancroft. Esq., who pointed out that a large amount of money had been paid ha the shape of interest upon the apecial loans which had been effected instead of creating new shares, or calling up capital on the old shares, when the works were extended three years ago. The amount of money paid in this way was in reality equivalent to a dividend of 2. per cent., and notwithstand- ing this a satisfactory profit had bees realized, which had enabled the directors to reduce the liabilities of the com- pany by about £3,500. He concluded that this was the wisest application of these profits at the present juncture, and he felt sure that the prudent course the directors had adopted would recommend itself to every shareholder, because it Gould not fail to consolidate the interests of the concern, and permanently enhanoe the value of the com- pany's shares.—The motion was unanimously passed.—The retiring direeters, Mr. Peter Bancroft and Mr. Robert Cook, were re-elected ; and Messrs. Stead, Taylor and Stead were re-appointed auditors to the company.—A vote of thanks to the chairman brought the meeting to a close, KAY'S COMPOuND, for Coughs and Ce3,ds, id equally se': vle•eable for Horses and Cattle.—.44rt.

TEMPORARY AUTHORITY TO SELL AT RUNCORN.—On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, the niagistrates granted temporary authority to sell intoxicating liquors at the beer- house called the George and Dragon to John Burgess. The house has recently been occupied by Henry Dixen. WIDNES AND TUE SHIP CANAL —Mr. F. H. Gossage, chairman of Widnes Local Board, has summoned a meeting of the ratepayers and property owners of the district, at the Local Board offices, on Wednesday next, " for the purpose of considering, if thought desirable, of approving and giving consent to the opposing by the Loc il Bard" of a bill con- ferring additional powers on the London and North-Western R tilway Comp my, and a bill for the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal. THE LATE Mn. J. JESSOP, OF WIDNES.—The remains of Mr. J. Jessop, of Widnes, who died in the 76th year of his age, on Priday last, were interred at Widnes Parish Church on Monday. He had held the office of parish clerk and registrar of marriages at Widnes Parish Church for upwards of 20 years, and the esteem in which he is hell was shown by the fact that the funeral was attended by a nu:nher of the prominent church officials and parishioners. The burial service was read by the Rev. G. H. Duggan. FORTHCOMING CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—Mr. J. Ravens. croft, whose services as organiat at Bethesda Congrega- tional Chapel, for the past year, have been highly appre- ciated, will give an evening concert in lietheda school- room on Monday, the 26th instant. He. has secured the services of Miss Annie Richardson, of the Liverpool concerts, and of several well known local amateurs of ability ; and, considering the excellent programme which has been provided, a good audience may be expected. PROPOSED CANAL FROM STOKE-ON-TRENT TO RUNCORN. —The North Staffordshire Chamber of Commerce has re- solved to petition Parliament in favour of the Manchester and Liverpool Ship C mal. The Chamber has also under con- sideration a scheme for connecting the Potteries with Liverpool by a ship cant! from Stoke-on-Trent to Runcorn. It would be about 20 miles in length, the estimated cost being £200,000, and it would enable ships of 200 tons burden to come from Liverpool. FUNERAL OF Mns. JONES, OF HALTON.—The remainsof Mrs. Mary Jones, of Holly Bank Halton, were interred, on Saturday last, at Runcorn Parish Church. Mrs. Jones was connected with an old Cheshire family, and was the widow of the late Mr. Richd. Jones, for many years collector to the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, at Runcorn. The body was placed in the family vault in the churchyard, a beauti- ful wreath of dowers being enclosed. The burial service was read by the Rev. John Lockwood, vicar of Halton. div.head: Xetter to the editor.
div.p: Xetter to the editor.
DR, STEELE AND THE COMMISSIONERS.

Sir.-1 was great surprised on reading your report of the last meeting of the Runcorn Commissioners. I was unaware that the Board possessed in its chairman the embodiment of so many essentials as to suggest to the mind the sobriquet of the younger Pitt, "the heaven-born minister." It seems almost a national loss that his power of governing was not earlier known or developed, as some constituency might have sent him to St. Stephens, and secured for him the. favourable attention of the Premier. No hesitancy would have been felt at the proposed retirement of the Speaker, and with the chairman of the Run- -corm Commissioners as Speaker of the House of Commons, Messrs. Parnell, Biggar, Healy, and other Hibernian orators would have been simply nowhere. New Procedure rules would have been unnecessary, the cloture would have occasioned no. difficulty, and two ses- sions would have been redeemed from barrenness. His resolution and powers of repression seem to be immense, and were finely displayed in his treatment of two members of the Board—Dr. MacDoitgall and Mr. Rhodes. His itera- tions that they were "out of order," and that discussion at meetings of the Board was out of place and could not be allowed, were to them simply astounding, and it was not long ere due effect was produced by Dr. MacDougsll throw- ing up the sponge in the unequal contest, and exclaiming, "if you rule me out of order, I submit." What followed 1 know not, but methinks an eye-witness of ability could easily have produced some entertaining ".pen and pencil "sketches in illustration of Burns' famous lines- -0 vp.cl om e power the giftie gie us To see oursels as others see us It woots! frae monie a blunder free us, And foolish notion. Yours, APOST LE OF ORDER. Runcorn, February 12th, 1883.

div.head: BRUTAL BED-FELLOW.
div.p: A BRUTAL BED-FELLOW.
WOUNDING CASE AT WIDNES.

On Tuesday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. mo. Brock, a powerful-looking fellow named Thomas Quinn, was brought up in custody charged with having on the previous night unlawfully wounded John Clark. The pro- secutor was unable to appear, and Inspector Barnett related the facts of the case. The prosecutor and the prisoner are navvies, lodging together in a house in Wellington-street. They slept in the same bed-room. On Monday night they returned borne about 10 o'clock after having been drinking, and they ascended to the bed-room. The prosecutor sat on the bed when the prisoner seized an earthenware chamber utensil and struck the former a blow on the head inflicting a wound four inches long, and cutting an artery. The wound penetrated to the bone, and blood flowed profusely. He was attended by Dr. McLennan, and subsequently the prisoner was apprehended by P.C. Sinner. who charged him with unlawfully wounding his companion. He replied "We both fell against the window." The injured man stated in the presenle of the prisoner that the latter, after striking him on the head, attempted to throw him through the window into the street below, and succeeded in putting him half way throue,h. The window frame and panes of glass were broken. The prisoner was .on this evidence remanded until the following day, when he was brought before Mr. H. Onkel!, senior, and Mr. John Brock. P.C. Skinner deposed that he had seen the injured man that morning. He was in so weak a state that lie ceuld not walk, and on the applica- tion of Superintendent Barker, the prisoner was remanded for a week.

div.head: BISHOP FRASER AM) TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN.
div.p: BISHOP FRASER AM) TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN.

The congregation ot Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn, have sent the following .letter of sympathy to the Lord Bishop of Manchester, signed by the clergy and church officials, con- sequent upon his Lordship's refusal to institute an avowed Ritualist as successor to the notorious Mr. Green :—" Lord Bishop,—We, the undersigned. on behalf of the congregation of Holy Trinity, Runcorn, beg to express our sympathy with your Lordship in the faithful discharge of an unpleasant duty, and to thank you for the bold stand you have taken in support of the principles of the Reformed Church of Eng- land. We conceive it to be a bishop's bounden duty to drive away all erroneous and strange doctrines, and not to foster or encourage or b 3 indifferent to the existence of such, and we could not but believe that one who ha 2 written as your Lordship has done regarding some of those dangerous doctrines, •to wit, auricular con confession, and priestly judicial absolution, ' that they are comtrary to the mind of the Church of England, and can- not be proved by any just or rational interpretation of her formularies,' would refuse to countenance them by refusing to institute a cleryman holding and prepared to teach such errors. With your Lordship we desire peace in the church, but we affirm it to be impossible so long as clergymen re- pudiate the authority of their Bishop, bid defiance to the laws of the realm, or refuse to to be ruled by the principles of the Prayer Book. We de not desire to contract the just limits of the Church of England, but a limit must be placed somewhere. It is impossible that Gospel truth and erroneous doctrine which subverts it can be allowed an existence, and be permitted to be taught by opposing parties in the Church ;that i, that legalities and illegalities shall co-exist as if they were alike. Nor can it be allowed that customs which have been in existence in the Church for ages, and have never been condemned by the law, but have been acquiesced in by all (although they may not , have the direct sanction of the law), are to be placed on a, level with the doctrines, and customs condemned by the law. Trusting that your. Lordship mty long be spared to protect the old Church of England against the conspiracy to re-impose popery in the Church of England '—as the late Archbishop of Canterbury and the present Bishop of Bath and Vells have put it," Ste. The following is the r3ply of Bishop Feaser Manchester, February 12th, 1883: Dear Sir,—l thank you for your words of sympathy which you have sent me in your own name, and in behalf. of the congregation of Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn. I will be glaclif yon.will express to them my gratitude. As the matter has now entered the legal stage, my business is ' simply to await the decision of the properly authorized tribunal with as little wish to stir up any agitation on the question as possible. Believe me to remain," &c.
The ofticial return of the expenses of the candidates at Liverpool in the recent Ir'y-election is published. Mr. Smith, M.P., expended £6,01., and Mr. A. B. Forwood 5d,010..

It l& again stated that Sir Robert Phillimore is about to resign the office of one of the judges in the Probate, Divorce, and Admiralty Division of the High Court of Justice. He will probably be succeeded by Mr. C. P. Butt, M.P., Q C. Sir Robert was admitted an advocite at Doctors' Commons in the year 1830.

_LATEST NEWS.

• The Russian, Turkish, and Austrian ambassadors visited Lord Granville at the Foreign Office yesterday. James Wilkie, railway foreman, was killed at Lightbill Goods Station, Glasgow, yesterday morning. Cardinal MiCabe was much better yesterday. The doctors state that there is a decided improvement. A Sydney correspondent telegraphs the death o 2 Dr. O'Connor, the Roman Catholic Bishop of Ballarat. At the Mansion House, London, yesterday.- Henry Cattell, bookseller and publisher, of Fleet-street, was 'committed for trial on a charge of selling the Christmas number of the Freethinker

The Gacette announces the confirmation of the Victoria Cross upon Private Fred Corbett,Third Battalion Kingalloyal Rifle Corps, for gallant conduct in attending Lieutenant Howard Vyse, mortally wounded during the reconnaisanee upon Kafrdovrar' sth August. Yesterday three Glendale, Skye, crofters John Macpherson, John Mornson, and John MacLeod—were arrested at Glasgow, at their hotel, by Mr. McTavish, messenger-at-arms. They appeared much surprised and depressed. Mr. Dongal, McKechine, and Mr. Geo. Barnet, advocates, are retained for the defence of the nseni who were taken V rail to Edinburgh. Six' valuable foxhounds, purchased by Mr. John Gubbins, master of the Limerick foxhounds, were poisoned yesterday near Croom. The farmers of the neighbourhood recently published notices to the effect that they had determined that no fox hunting should take place this year. Seven hounds of the same pack were lately poisoned near Rathkeale. Mr. Gubbins, it is stated, has decided to give up bunting in Ireland.

fiTHE GOVERNMENT OF EGYPT.—Parliamentary papers. issued yesterday, include three on are Egyptian question, the most important of which appears•to be No.2', containing the correspondence respecting the reorganisation in Egypt. In this, Lord Dufferin, replying to Earl Granville's-request for an opinion as to the establishment in Egypt of institu- tions favourable to the prudent development of liberty, says the general current of opinion appeared unfavourable to the reconstitutitm of the Chamber of Notables, and in- dicates his preference for some such. system as exists in India.

THE REPORTED ARREST OF IRISH MEMBERS. There is ne truth whatever in the report that two Irish members of Parliament have been arrested. It is true, how- ever, that detectives are carefully watching the movements of certain prominent members of the Land League. In August last some Land League documents, including, accounts, got into the possession of the Dublin Detective Department.
THE SMA.LLWOOD TRAGEDY. DEATII.OF THE SECOND -VICTIM.

Mary Moran, the second victim of the Smallwood mur— derer, died yesterday morning at about ten o'clock. Be- yond the few words she is said to have uttered early on Tuesday morning, nothing further has been elicited front her. She has since lain in a perfectly unconscious condi- tion. No arrests have been made in the neighbourhood of the tragedy, but the police are confident of ultimate 'success.

div.head: SUPPOSED LOSS OF THE BYWELL CASTLE. AND
div.p: SUPPOSED LOSS OF THE BYWELL CASTLE. AND
FORTY. LIVES.

The latest telegrams received from Lloyd's, yesterday, make no mention of the arrival of the steamer Bywell Castle, 1,376 tons register, homeward bound from the Mediterranean to Hall with a full cargo of produce, and the underwriters have given up all hopes as to her safety. She passed Gibralta on the 28th January all well, and was seen the day following day off* the Spanish Coast, but has not been heard of since. There stems no doubt now that she has foundered in the Bay of Biscay during the hurricane of the 2nd February, and that the whole of her crew have perished.

HOUSE OF LORDS.

ALLEGED MISREPRESENTATION.—The Marquis Of SALTS-. BURY complained that the Foreign Secretary had last night misrepresented what be had said in his Edinburgh speech, and justified what he said there.—Lord GRANVILLE de- clined to apologise, and insisted upon the authority of various passages from Hansard that he had not in any way misrepresented the noble Marquis.—After a few words from the Lord Chancellor, the subject dropped. THE WAR IN EGYPr.—The LORD CHANCILLOR read a letter from Lord Alcester acknowledging the vote of thanks to himself, and his officers, seamen, and marines in Egypt. —Adjourned. --

HOUSE OF COMMONS. NEW WHIT.—A new writ was ordered to be issued for Newcastle-on-Tyne. No-ricEs.—Mr.RYLatins gave notice on an early day he would call attention to the present state of the National expenditure, and to move a resolution.—Mr. SEXTON (Jaye notice to ask whether the Government intended to retain Mr. George Bolton, who lately appeared in a law court in England, in the service of the Crown in Ireland. THE TRANSVAAL.—Mr. ASHLEY, replying to Sir M. H. BEACH, said the Transvaal Government had not yet paid the £50,000 which it had been arranged should be paid by the end of the year 1882. Further papers would be pre- sented which would give all the information in possession of the Government.
TUE SKYE CROFTERS.—The LORD ADVOCATE, replying to Sir G. Campbell, said before anything was done with regard to the Scotch crofters, the present law must be vindicated as it stood.

Mn.. BRADLAUDIL—In reply to Mr. Newdegate, the SPEAKER said the resolutions passed as to the non-admis- sion of Mr. Bradlaugh to take the path lapsed at the close of last session.—Mr.NEWDECIATE wished to know whether the Government intended taking steps to prevent Mr. Bradlaugh appearing at the table to take the oath.—The MARQUIS of Hawn/carol; said steps to prevent Mr. Bradlaugh coming to the table did not fall within the province of the Govern- ment. It was a question for the House to settle. THE DEEATE ON THE ADDRESS. The adjourned. debate on Sir Wilfrid Lawson's amendment to , the Address was resented by Mr. A. BALPOUR, who. utterly condemned the E4ytian policy ef the Government. He contended the Government went to war with Egypt to protect British bondholders and British in- terests, and that, therefore, they must continue that pro- tection, else British blood and treasure had been spent in vain, Ile moved to amend the amendment to the effect that the House iregretted the Government had not acted with. energy at first; whereby war would have been avoided and British interests preserved. Mr. Nownicarst , seconded the proposed amendment of the amendment. Mr. RICHARD said the Government were now doing away with the Control in Egypt which they went to war to sup- port. Had that Control been so modified as to have given the Egyptian people even tho semblance of self-government, war would have been averted. He should support the original amendment.—Mr. CnAlw.atte denied that the Con- servative party stimulated the Government to embark in the war, and said the object of the meeting held at Willis's rooms was to condemn the weak and feeble policy of the Government.— Mr. RYTANDS, while entertaining the opinkn that the circumstances under which Alexandria was bombarded was a gross act of national immorality, could-not, vote for the amendment ; and further, he believed that the moving such an amendment to the Address was not the proper way of raising the question of the past policy of the Government. He did not see how it was possible for England to at once withdraw her troops front Egypt. She had assumed a certain responsibility, and from the country she could not withdraw until that responsibility was. fulfilled.— Mr. GORST supported the amendment, and strongly censured tho actions of the Government as regarded its Egyptian policy. [LIFT SITTING.]

rA NUISANCE. Sir.—While giving a full share of my -sympathy to the, "British workman "-rod the "horny-handed son of toil," I don't think it right they should have everything thfir own way, but thattthey should be taught to give and take a little. Doesn't -my complaint come under the head of " Nuisances ?" a live in a street in which likewise live a number of people whose occupation, I •uaume, requires their attention at an early hour; yes, as-early as halt -past three the row begins. Rat-tat-tat-tat; bammet, hammer, hammer, hammer; " Hi, hi, hi, hi; Mr. --So-and-so, Mr. So- and-so ;" "Hei, hoi," from the inside of the house • "All right " from the outside. This in a bees voice, Of shrill and penetrating quality, followed by footsteps, heard dis- tinctly in the night, and a few doors of the same row and hammering is repeated. I'm done for; my rest is broken, and my temperament tells me there's no more sleep for poor me. I dose and fret for half an hour, and thin a man re- peats at about four other houses the same " Chihike." I dose again, and then at half-past five the hooter or hooters pierce the space to call the workmen. At six o'clock the same, -or other hooters do the like, so that by the time it's neces- sary for poor-me to rise, I'm dazed, fidgety. nervous, and done up. Went of sleep and broken rest render me utterly unfit for my occupation, which is gone about in a listless and imperfect manner, and all from no fault of my own. I've said nothing of shattered health, but experience tells me that I shell be driven away to seek that repose at night that every man has a right to expect wherever he'e loca- ted. If a man goes home in the early hours of the morning and shouts and hammers at a door or doors, the policeman properly interferes, and locks him up for being A nuisance to his neighbours. Where's the difference? I see none, except that the former is the worst because it is persistent. It is not for me to suggest by what more quiet means the workman should be hailed to his toil, but I do think that the authorities—either the police or nuisance inspector— should see that brains have as much claim to consideration in St. Helens an they receive in other places, and that muscles shouldn't have it all their own way.—l remain, sir, yours trulee, SENSITIVE. St. Helens, Feb, 1582.

WARRINGTON AND LIVERPOOL WATER WAY VERSUS THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. Sir,—Since the end of this Manchester scheme, together with a Warrington proposal, is by those well informed be- lieved now to be a fore-gone conclusion, and the proles- eional engineering skill, so far as at present made public, is utterly unable todevise or provide a satisfactory water car- riage between Warrington and Liverpool by the river Mersey, free from landlords and other objections, cuttings, dredgings, clrc., at a cost of £BO,OOO, exclusive of a weekly after charge of £LOOO for dredging (and which fact may not generally be known to the public), allow an unpro- fessional to say tbat this desirable water carriage can be had by vessels of from 200 t 0.300 tonnage of displacement, both ways quickly, every day and night, without reference to the Old Canning Dock sill tide register at Liverpool, and, with leave, guaranteed within twelve months, any old method of dredging (removing one lay for a return deposit of the next) or, any expense for improving the natural facilities of the river beyond sowe £lO,OOO, when it will afford all here named, its utility baing then scientifically applied. This statement can be disputed, but not disproved, by any ship canal or river engineers, whether professors impractical, or amateurs practical. The substitute for dredging avoids what in the Manchester scheme might have been fatal, to any profits, save a kind of professional provision. The facts and practicability of this project can be substantiated by skillful testimony beyond all doubt, provided the present natural elements and conditions remain. In conclusion, this invention may be kept private until the final issue of other river hobbies are by Parliament or other ways disposed of. I enclose my card, and for worthy considerations would disclose this plan.—Yours truly, CRUX CRITICORUSI. Liverpool and Warrington, 13th Feburary, 1883.

SUPPOSED SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS. - On Wednesday afternoon an irquest was held at the " Fingerpost " public-Louse, Pair, before Mr. Barker, coroner, touching the death of a man named Samuel Cook, who was drowned in the canal on Monday.—Sarah Cook, the widow of the deceased, said her husbard was 52 years of age, and had lived at 8, Baxter-street, Parr. On Monday Afternoon be left home about half-past two in the afternoon, saying that he would be back about rive, but she did not see him again till he was brought back dead. When he left 'home he was perfectly sober, having only had one pint of beer. There had been nothing to trouble him at home and they had always lived comfortably together. He had never attempted his own life.—Mrs. Ellen irook said she lived on the canal bank east, near the ship Inn. She had not known the deceased before his death not even by sight, but on Mon- day evening, between half-past six and seven o'clock, she saw him standing on the canal bink, between the rails and the water His back was to the water and he had hold of the rails with his bands. This was just in front of the Ship Inn, the landlord of which just came out at the moment she was looking at deceased, and spoke to her about the markets. She turned for a moment or two towards the landlord, and on looking round again saw the el2ceased was missing. She ran to the canal edge and there saw hi:n floating on the water face down; and she at once gave an alarm, and ran into her house for a clothes prop. On coming out again she sSw that some people had got a ladder, and were trying to save the drowning man by means of it, but he never made any attempt to lay hold of it. The people round abut told her that it was only a black dog that was in the ivater, and it. hurt her feelings very mach when they said it. Ultimately deceased was got out by means of grappling irons, but be was quite dead. He had been in the water about half an hour, but she could not say that he might have been got out sooner if more strenuous efforts had been made. Her own opinion was that deceased had committed suicide, because be seemed to have gone deliberately into the water without naking any splash. On being questioned, witness said she bad first seen deceased come from the Ship Inn door and go across towards the canal as if he were drunk, and then he must have gone through under the rails. He did not struggle in the water, or seem to make any effort to save himself.—Henry Fisher, who lives in Raven-street, spoke to having- heard, on Monday evening, some children say that a man was in the - "cut." He went there, and saw deceased in the water and assisted to drag him out.—Mr. Cooks, who was recalled, said her husband had been in the habit of sometimes taking a good Ceal of drink, but she had never seen him very much the worse of it.—The Coroner, in summing up, said the jury would have to decide whether in their opinion the death had been accidental or it had been a suicide. The evidence rather pointed to a suicide, as the man must have got through under the railings, but on the oth..r hand there seemed to be ne motive for his committing suicide.—Some conversation then ensued amongst the jurymen, in the course of which one of them gave it as his opinion that it was scarcely possible for a man to sink if he was well filled with whiskey. a statement which caused some amusement. The same juryman also held that the saying that a drown- ing man would catch at a straw was fallacy, as he had on two or three occasions put a staff into the hands of dros%ning Persona who would not lay hold cf it. A fellow-juryman. however, pointed out that there was a difference between a staff and a straw. Ultimately a verdict that deceased had committed suicide, but that there was no evidence to show in what state of mind he had been, was come to.

GOOD TIi3fPLARS' MEETING.—The usual weekly session of the Hope of Earlistown Lodge of Good Templars was held in the lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Monday evcnlng last. There was a very good attendance, and Brother Geo. E. Warburton, W.C.T., presided. After the opening formali- ties, one new member was initiated, and several items of business were discussed, including one in conuection with the arrangements being made for a united temperance demonstration in a few weeks. Afterwards Brother T. Gorse capitally gave a song, and the chairman excellently recited "A temperance speech." The meeting closed about the usual hour, half-past nine. THE BLUE RIBBON AND GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MOVE- INIENT.—A very enjoyable and successful gathering, in connection with the Golborne Blue Ribbon and Gospel Temperance Movement was held in the Congregational schoolroom, on Friday evening last, when a party of ladies and gentlemen from Glazebury attended and gave an excellent entertainment. The chair was occupied by Mr. Potts, of Glazebury. The songs, recitations, &c., which were given were capitally rendered, and were much appre- ciated by those present, who really had a treat. A deserving vote of thanks to the performers was accorded at the close of the entertainment. KAY'S COMPOUND, for Colds and Coughs. Compositon and strength en each bottle. Bold by Chemists. After the wretched weather experienced of late, a brie day was thoroughly enjoyed by the large number of folks who patronised the opening day's coursing at Haydock Park; and as there was nothing of importance clashing with this popular fixture, a good company paid for admission to the picturesque aroud. The programme put forth consisted of a 64 and two 32 dog stakes. Although each of the stakes was drawn on Monday afternoon, the Waterloo Trial Plate was left over until the second day, the order of running being once through the Maiden States and Haydock Lodge States, a total of 48 courses. The ground was in splendid order, considering the quantity of rain that has fallen of late; and although coursing was not commenced before nearly half-past eleven o'clock, the day's sport was brought to a close in capital time. There were not many pretty displays in the Maiden Stakes. Irene, Musician, Maggie, Crown Jewel, Born a Lady, Nellie. and Limerick, however, showed a bit of form, and an excuse must be made for Mr. Pilking- ton's bitch Philomena, who, in addition to being in season, was rather unluckily put out by Drury Lowe, who had all the luck in a short trial, In the Haydock Lodge Stakes, Pericles, ChrisLine,Hetty, Avonmore, and Alpine all deserve a. word of praise for their smart running, especially Haw, Avonmore, and Christine, who ran in very clever style. Appended is a return of the day's coursing : The MAIDEN STAKES, for 64 All Ages, at £4 103 each. Winner, £110; second, £5O; third and fourth, £l6 each; four winners of three courses, £8 each; and eight winners of two courses, £1 each. _

SUNDAY DRINKING AT EARLFSTOWN.—At the Newton Town Hall on Monday last, before T. J. Gillespie, Esq., ' Martin Burke was charged with being drunk and incapable at Earlestown on the previous day. P.C. Ivison moved the case, and the prisoner was fined 5s and costs.—Wm. Smith was charged with being drunk in Crow-lane on Sunday. P.C. Spencer deposed that the prisoner gave a wrong name and address. He was fined 5s und casts. THE CARETAKER OF THE LIBERAL CLUB.—As will be well known to the majority of our readers, the committee of the Earlestown and District Liberal Club have decided upon removing from their present premises in Market-street, Earlestown, to a more commodious and convenient building in Fairclough-street. In view of this a suitable man and his wife were advertised for as caretekees to live on the premises. and the consideration of the applications received came before the committee on Tuesday evening last. When it is gated that no less than 43 applications were received, it will be seen that the task of selection was no light o4e The terms, testimonials, &c., of each were duly cone' and the number was first reduced te twelve. T it) two— weret• afterwards brought down to four. e— -men adjourned both Earlestown residents. The mee'ene final appointment until this (Saturday) after" will be made. ~,e.sta AT THE EARLSTOWN WESLEYAN SEnviralie choir of the Brunswick Wesleyan Methodist Ciefei, Cross-lane, Earlestown, assisted by a number of the sahool children, gave a service of song, entitled, "Gideon, in that place of worship on Sunday afternoon last. There was a very large attendance of teachers, scholars, and mem- bers of the congregation, the proceeds being devoted to the new organ fund. Miss M. E. Greenall presided at the har- monium, while the singing was conducted by Mr. Thomas Clare in the absence of Mr; tiugh Parr, who recently met with an unfortunate accident which prevented him from taking his accustomed position as leader. Arl!-. Burgess read the connective readings. After the proceedings had been opened with singing and prayer, an introduction was nicely given by Miss Greenall, after which the choir gave " 01.), God, how weak, how poor, how lone." The connective read- ing then referred to the sin ana punishment of the people of Israel, and in the niece, " Ye have sinned," Mr. Sam Swann giving the bass solo, most excellently acquitted himself. the alto solo was finely rendered by Miss M. A. Parr, and the chorus by the choir was also well given. ruring the service, "God is our refuge and strength," was effectively given as a quartette by Miss M. A. Parr, Miss Walton, Mr. Gibson, and Mr. Thomas Gilmore; and the choir sang "How can we stand before Thee, Lord ? " and "Oh put away the veil." The soprano solo in "What proofs of mercy was most sweetly sun..' by Miss Lydia Sides, and "Oh, not by rengt 11," "Father of all," and "Crud, our Lord, goes on before us," by the &Join The next musical niece was Sweet is the calm," including an alto solo by Miss A. Swann, which was beautifully rendered; the whole con- cluding with the anthem, "Sing unto the Lord," a brilli- intly execnted performance by the choir. A collection at the close realised over X-5.

DRUNKENNESS AT EAHLEStOWN.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on SaturdAy last, Thomas liinread was tined se. and costs for beipg drunk, at Wargrave, on the 29th Jan.— John Broderick was also fined a like amount for being drunk and disorderly, at Earlestown. on the 27th -L,ouary.—Thos. Duddle was summoned for hp;ns drunk, on the 3rd inst., at Earlestown, and was also tined ss. and cotos.—Alice Wood- cock was charged with creating a disturbance in Fairclougb- street, Earlestown, on the 19th January, and was bound over to keep the peace for six months; THE LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION.—An arrangement has been made which will relieve Sir Stafford Northcote of the more arduous portion of his duties as leader of the Oppobi- tion. The medical advisers of the right honourable gentle- man have warned him against over work, and in conse- quence it has been settled that Mr. Smith, Sir Richard Cross, irid Lord John Manners shall from time to time relieve Sir Stafford in order to obviate the necessity of his staying late at the House. At the same time Sir S. Northcote expects to be present on all important occasions.

FORTH COMING TEMPE RAN C E MISSION AT EARLESTOWN.— Arrangements are being made for a special temperance mis- sion to be conducted in Earleetown during the tirst week in March. All the various temperance organisations ge taking part, and several popular and well-known temperancr speakers ard workers have been invited, and are ex- pected to be:present and address the meetings which will be held.

SELLING UNWEIGHED BREAD.—James Profit Was charged with having. on the 19th ult., sold a loaf of bread otherwise than by weight. William George Daniels stated that on the day named he went to de!endaut's shop and asked for a 41b loaf, and the defendant's daughter, a youpg girl, supplied him with the loaf produced without weighing It. P.O. Antrobus proved having weighed the loaf, which he found to be 3 ozs. light. Defendant said be gave instructions to his wife and daughter always to weigh the bread. He had scolded his daugh- ter tcr not weighing the loaf mentioned, and site said site had forgotten to do it. A .fine of 103 and costs was imposed.— Josiah Owen. for having committed a similar offence on the 3rd instant was also fined 103 and costs. The loaf was found to be 2 ozs. light. • Matrix WHILST IN CHARGE OF A HOWIE AND TRAP —NtoSe3 Walke,, of Warrington, w as charge .1 with havrng, on the 13th ult., been drunk whilst in charge of a horse and.trap at Booth's Hill.
