div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

LIVELY MEETING AT RUNCORN. 1 A public meeting, convened by the Runcorn Ratepayers' Association, was held in Bethesda school-room, on Monday evening, for the purpose of considering the advisability or otherwise of forwarding a petition to °both Houses of Par- liament, asking that the standing orders might be suspended with regard to the Manchester Ship CAnal, so th.t the scheme might be considered in committee during the present session of Parliament. At the request of the association, Mr. Riley attended on behalf of Messrs. Grundy, Kershaw, and Co., solicitors to the scheme ; and Mr. Herbert Birch, on behalf of the Provisional Committee, to explain the position of affairs, and answer any questions that might be asked. Mr. H. Coleburn, president of tbe association, pre- sided, and there was a large attendance. 1)r. McDougall and Mr. Horsfall occupied seats on the platform. The CHAIRMAN related the causes which had led to the calling of the meeting, and remarked that after the refusal of the Commissioners to consider the question, the associa- tion thought the matter ought not to be slighted, but should come before the ratepayers at large. Ile called upon Mr. RILEY, who said the object of the meeting was of a technical character, and did not involve the whole of the Manchester Ship Canal project. He explained the reason why the Examiner on Standing Orders had thrown out the Bill, laecause they had not deposited plans of the works in- tended to be executed in the estuary of the Mersey from Runcorn to Liverpool. If that decision WAS allowed to rest, the scheme would be delayed twelve months, and to obviate that, petitions such as the chairman had read to the meeting, had been extensively signed by numerous public bodies, and he thought he might say, by thousands of individuals pray- ing the Houses of Parliament, under the circumstances, to suspend the standing orders, which they had ample power to do. The promoters viewed the scheme as truly one of national importance, and he had no doubt the inhabitants of Runcorn regarded it not only as a matter of national im- portance, but of most serious importance to the prosperity of their town and port. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He pointed out that by adopting the desired petition, Runcorn would still retain the privilege of going before Parliatrent and opp9sing, or asking for any clause to be inserted in the Bill. They pledged themselves to nothing with regard to their own interests, and he hoped those present, and numerous other ratepayers who were not present, would sign the petition. He had some reason to believe that the Commissioners might be induced to call a special meeting at which they would probably affix their seal to a similar petition—(bear, hear)—and if they bad the petition signed by the ratepayers individually, and were strengthened by a petition signed by the duly constituted authorities of the town, they would have got, Le was quite sure, as much as the town and port of Runcorn could give them, and they would feel much indebted to those who had been good enough to sign. Dr. MacDouGaLL moved the followin, resolution:—"That the forms of petition to the House of Cords and House of Commons, read by the chairman, praying that the standing orders of the two Houses in respect to the Manchester Ship Canal Bill may be suspended. be approved and signed." He said to those - people who were interested in the prosperity of the town, it must be apparent, if they looked back to the history of Runcorn for the last 25 years, that the policy adopted by the leaders of public opinion with the London and North.- I Western Railway Company when they projected their rail- way from Bi:-cilwo)d Junction to Ditton, w.s an ex.:;:ulin,4l3-

div.head: EXAARNEP, SATURDAY, FEtRUARY 17, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAARNEP, SATURDAY, FEtRUARY 17, 1883.

RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS AND THE SHIP CANAL. A special meeting of the Board of Commissioners, to con- sider the advisability of affixing the seal of the Board te the petition to Parliament for dispensing with the standing orders in the case of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, wes held yesterday afternoon. Dr. Steel presided, and there were also present :—Messrs. NV. Rhodes, W. Fisher, J. Mea- dow croft, J. WilHerne, W. Shaw, 3. Pritchard, Dr. 3iacDeugall, J. J. Speakman, J. W. Lightburn, W. Whit- taker, W. H. Linaker elaw clerk), W. Brookes (secretary), and Barker (surveyor). The CHAIRMAN said this matter came before the Board at the lest meeting, but in an irregular manner, and the members had no power to discuss it then. It was propord that the Board adjonra to discuss the question, but the motion was defeated. Since then he had thought that as the proposed construction of the canal was of momentous importance to Runcorn, it was well that the Board should meet and discuss the question, and decided whether they should affix the seal of the Board to the petition. At the suggestion of the Chairman, Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN moved that the Board consider the matter in committee, but as there was no seconder, the proposal fell to the ground. Mr. L/GHTEURN said as he understood the affixing the seal of the Board to the petition would not affect any friendly opposition that they might have to offer the bill to secure the rights and interests of Runcorn. In his opinion there were two views in which this question might be considered. The first was of an engineering character— could the canal be made? and the second: If so, will it permanently benefit Runcorn? There was no doubt that the expenditure of two millions or three millions of pounds of money wouli benefit Runcorn for the period during which the works were proceeding, but would it benefit the town permanently? The engineers stated on one hand that the canal could be made without interfering with the water- way, and on the other hand they had it on equally good authorities that it could not be made. Therefore when any proposition could not be conclusively proved it became an experiment, and when they experimented in a waterway like the Mersey, and the experiment failed, by sanding up the mouth of the river, what would be the state of affairs? Why, there would be no one to remove the training walls, and that would be a matter of great importance to Runcorn, and Liverpool too. They would wish to see a deposit of money for the removal of the walls in case they did not answer well. That, however, the company was not prepared to do. %But he had no doubt that it the canal was made, and they got deep water at Runcorn, or in other words, Run- corn were brought nearer the sea, it would improve the town to a great extent. [Mr. Sweev : Hear, hear.] Mr. Light- burn pointed out that if they did not affix the seal to the petition, the discussion of the scheme in Parliament might be delayed for a year, and he moved "that a petition be signed." Mr. Frsana seconded the motion. In reply to Mr. Lightburn, the LAW CLERK said that if the seal were affixed to the petition the Board could offer any opposition either hostile or friendly. Mr. H. SHAW said he took it that the subject was rather more important than had bees stated, because if all that had been stated in favour of signing the petition was all that could be stated for it, it seemed to him a loss of time dis- cussing the matter—(hear, hear)—that was, if the best that could be said for putting the seal of the Board to that erpetition Was that it did not prevent them from opposing the scheme afterwards for the purpose of securing the rights which the people of Runcorn were entitled to. It seemed to be clear to everyone that it would only leave them where they were; therefore what was the use of going to the trouble of discussing the question? He should have been pleased if the proposer of the resolution had endeavoured to show them that they would not be worse off by any action of the Board that day. The real question was, what bad stopped the Bill and jeopardised it at present? So far as Warrington and Manchester, which were on the banks of the canal, were concerned, they had deposited before them the plans which showed them in every sense where they would be benefited or otherwise by the scheme; therefore, up to that point, there had been no difficulty. It was merely a question in this case of purchasing the right of land, and taking the water and so forth. What Runcorn had to consider before they did anything in the matter that day was what was prooresed by this scheme that would affect them. If be had thought it worth while to have snpported the petition, he should have sought some information, and he would have endeavoured to shew the Board that nothing was contemplated by the promoters of the scheme that would in any way prejudice the rights of persons engaged ic trade in the town. But there had been no attempt to show that the Canal Company would not interfere with their rights, but they had prac- tically shown them that they were willing to interfere with their rights. Mr. Shaw produced a copy of the bill in reference to the plans which had been deposited, and read the preamble, which showed that the channel was to take a line from Runcorn to Garston lighthouse. The company have not shown where they would put the channel between those two points, but they nevertheless in the bill proposed to acquire the right to make it anywhere between Runcorn and Garston without giving the Board any power to know how it was going to affect the interest of Runcorn. And it was just be- cause they had failed to show where that channel 11.0 to be that thm Examiner had refused to ViliCiw the bill to pass. He thought po man of business would ask the Committee of the House of Commons to dispense with that necessary safeguard which had been consiAered necessary, so that everybody should know the particulars relating to their interests. It was not merely a question of position, whether the canal should be on one side of the river or in the centre. From a plan he had before him it was clear that the deep cutting must go through the centre span of the Runcorn Bridge, for if they went to this side they could not get past "No Man's Land" with the deep cutting. Another point which was of great importance to Runcorn was this. It was known by every gentleman that had anything to do with the river, or had observed it, that the river enabled vessels with deeper draft to reach Runcorn than they could get on the other side. This was owing entirely to the "scour " from the waters coming down river and from the canals. If they took away all that slier water, all the water that came from the canals and from the brooks, then the deep would silt up. The canal company sought for powers to do these things. Mr. Shaw enumerated the brooks and streams the company sought to have control over, and asked where was all that water going to. It seemed to him there had been a mis- taken idea as to what the ship canal intended to do. If they were going to do what was done on the Clyde, then Runcorn would' be benefited. If the proposed channel was made 20 or 30 feet below the level of the river, into which all the water he had mentioned would be poured, all the works on the banks—Messrs. Bruedrit's and so oa—would be silted up in a month, because they would have taken a.way all the "scour." If the company had shown 14iern where the channel was to be formed, they might have had an idea what to ask for in o,,posing the but as the matter at present stood they were completely in the dark. Mr. Shaw concluded by etatine that it was an indignity to the engineer and the House of Commons to ask for the standing orders to be dispensed with, and declared that he should vote against the motion. Mr. RIIODES said it had been stated that if the Ship Canal were made Runcorn must necessarily be bene- fitted, but it had not been shown in what way. His im- pression was that it would be the reverse of that, for he took it that the town was largely dependent upon the traffic at the docks and the navigation canal. It was a fact known to many there that 99 per cent of the imports at the port of Ruccorn were not for Runcorn, but simply received there for transit. Now, the object of the Ship Canal was to takp vessels direct to Manchester and to Warrington, and he could not see what benefit Runcorn was to derive from seeing the vessels sail past the docks with merchandise to those parts. (Dr. MecDornetc: I ask what goods?) From something like 20,000 tons of China clay, glass, sand, and every description of raw material for Manchester and Warrington. At least 100,000 tons of pig iron passed through the port of Runcorn for Manchester and War- rington in a year. If that large quantity of material went direct, what was to become of the flats and the vessels and the port of Runcorn, for .what other trade could spring up in the place be could not see. They could not get any larger North Staffordshire trade, for they had it all now. Mr. LAZE said the question at issue was whether the Bill should be discussed this session or next session, and on whichever occasion it was Runcorn would have to oppose the Bill to protect themselves. Mr. MEADOWCROFr followed in a long speech, in which he took up the same ground as Mr. Shaw, and advised the Board to look the matter clearly in the face and tell the promoters that they refused to look upon the scheme ; characterising the proposal to sign the petition as a leap in the dark. They were told that if they sigated the petition they would net injure their future action. That seemed to him a most illogical conclusion, and referring to the meeting on Monday night, if meeting it could be termed_....... Dr. MecDouneu. objected to that expression. Mr. Suew said a meeting called on such short notice did not deserve the name. Dr. MacDoroser.i There were four days' clear nctice. Mr. MEADOWCROFT still adhered to the expression. Dr. STEELE closed the discussion by saving it was out of order, but if he had to state what he thought of the meet- ing he should be out of order too. (Laughter.) Mr. PRITCHARD said it was of vital importance that they should secure the channel on the Runcorn side, and, in his opinion, if they took any action at all, it ough-f to be one of watchful observation. Dr. MecDoncearx said there had been so much special pleading that one could not help regretting that it had taken place at that Board. Mr. Shaw had referred to the rights of persons in the town, but the rights of Runcorn were bound up in one powerful body which had entire right to the water courses coming into Runcorn from all direc- tions. It seemed to him, therefore, that that body was capable of taking care of itself. He ridiculed Mr. Shaw's statement with regard to " scouring " water, asking what the canal company would do with all the water in the canal. He remarked that he was not aware that the Bridgewater Navigation Company had so much effect upon the prosperity of Runcorn, for they employed comparatively few people in the town. He also was under the impression that the greater part of the pig iron went to North Staffordshire, and not to Manchester and Warrineton, and concluded by stating that before Parleiment wealth pais the scheme plans 1

would have to be deposited, and Runcorn might depend upon its rights being protected. Mr. LIGHTBURN having replied, the motion was carried by seven votes to seven, the petition being so altered that the plans would have to be deposited before the second reading of the Bill, if the standing orders were suspended.

WIDNES OWNERS AND OCCUPIERS' ASSOCIATION. ELECTION COMPROMISES. The annual general meeting of the members of the above association was held at the Drill Hail, on 'rlirirsday, for the purpose, the circular calling the meeting stated, of considering the action to be taken with regard to the en- suing elections. Major Cross presided, and there was a good audience. Amongst those present were the Rev. T. Finegan, Messrs. E. Carey, Dr. O'Keeffe, W. H. Kershaw, John Taylor, Francis Heyes, F. H. Pankhurst, Joshua Mid- wood, D. Wright, S. Owens (secretary of the Ratepayers and Property Owners' Association), J. W. Carlisle, J. Matthews, John Beech, Thomas Balmer, James Walker, W. Crabtree, Joseph Bagnall, and Frank Gaskell (secretary). The CHAIRMAN said it had been represented to the com- mittee of the association that they held their meetings at a time that was very inconvenient for the ratepayers of Widnes to attend—that they, so to say, carried on their proceedings in a sort of hole and corner fashion. The com- mittee were determined this time that that charge should I not be made against them, and a circular had been sent to each ratepeyer in the township calling upon them to attend the meeting that night, and speak upon any subject they pleased. They were all aware that there were five vacancies to till at the coming Local Board election, the retiring members being Dr. Booth, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Pankhurst, Shuttleworth, and Forster. Dr. Booth and Mr. Shuttleworth had declined to stand again, but the other gentlemen had intimated their willingness to serve if elected. The secretary, Mr. F. Gasket!, had received the following letter :—" Widnes Ratepayers' Association, February 13th, 1883. Dear sir,—ln answer to yours of the 6th inst., I beg to state that at a meeting of the Executive Committee of the above, on the 31st ult., it was resolved that—(l) Should the Owners and Occupiers' Association agree to a compro- mise, this association asks to lee allowed to nominate two representatives for election on the Local Board; (2) that no less a number will be satisfactory ; and (3) that in the event of failure in the negotiations, this association nomi- nates five candidates as last year. An early reply will oblige, yours respectfully, SAmUEL OWENs.—Frank Gaskell, Esq." Mr. Joael BEECH said the members of the Ratepayers' Association did not wish to put the town to the expense of a contest, and they would be pleased if the Owners and Occu- piers' Association would allow them to nominate hlr.Barnett Dutton and Mr. John Houghton in place of the two retiring members who would not stand for re-election. Should there be a contest the Ratepayera' Association would nom mate five c indidatee. Mr. CAREY, in order that a contest might be avoided, moved that the proposition contained in Mr. Owen's letter of the 13th February be accepted, and that Messrs. F. H. Pankhurst, D. Forster, John Houghton, Barnett, Dutton' and Dr. O'Keeffe be the members nominated to fill up the vacancies on tbe Local Board at the next election. Mr. BEECH seconded the proposition. Mr. HEYES inquired whether, if some outsider nominated another candidate, and a contest could not be avoided, the two associations would support the five gentlemen named. The Calmar( : I take that for granted. The Rate- payers' Aseociation make a proposition, and there can be no doubt that they will honourably carry out the agreement and do their best for it. Both associations will support these candidates as far as they can influence the rate- payers. If anyone chooses to nominate a candidate we cannot avoid it. Mr. BEECH: He would stand no chance. The motion was then unanimously carried. Mr. CAREY asked what about the Guardians' election, and the Rev. Father Finegan, Messrs. Matthews, Thome Sadler, and Gerrard, were mentioned as the candidates. The Rev. FATHER FINEGAN said before he came to the meeting he bad come to the conclusion to ask them to pro- vide a substitute for him on the Guardians. He stood last year to fill up a gap, and he had no wish then, nor had he now, to become the guardian for Widnes. The otlize entailed upon him a great amount of labour that was certainly not of the pieesantest character, and having, in his position as priest, such a large district to look after, he felt that it was more than could be expected of him. He had taken a lively interest in the School Board, and he wished to reserve him- self as a candidate for a seat with that body, feeling that he had not time to perform the duties of guardian as well as they should be performed. He should be very glad if they would select a member in his place and he would retire in favour of their choice. Mr. BEECH said the Rev. Father Finegan had most ably represented the wishes of the ratepayers at the Board of Guardians, and he hoped he would reconsider his decision, for if he did not stand there would be a contested election. Mr. J. %V. CARLILE, after a short conference with Father Finegan, said the rev, gentleman hid re-considered his decision, and was willing to place himself in the hands of the meeting, and he wood teand if it was their wish. (Loud applause.) He therefore moved that the Rev. Father Finegan, Messrs. Matthews, T. Sadler, and GerrArd be nominated as Guardians for the ensuing three years. Mr. PANKnuRsr had great pleasure in seconding the motion. Mr. OWENS remarked that the Ratepayers' Association had pledged themselves to support the candidature of the Rev. Father Finegan, Messrs. Thomas Sadler, Gerrard, and Samuel Sadler. He had just had a conversation with Mr. Samuel Sadler, who, considering the unanimity that pre- vailed in the meeting, willingly withdrew his name from the candidature. The Ratepayers' Association would gladly support the motion which had been proposed. ( epplauee.) The Rev. FATHER FINEGAN Said if his standing would save the expenses of an election, he would do so, on the dis- tinct understanding that he retired in favour of anyone who contested the seat. The CHAIRMAN spoke in high terms of praise of the rev. gentleman's services, and the motion being put to the vote, was carried unanimously. Dr. O'REEFFE said he reserved to himself the privilege of nominating members for the Local Board, and also for the Board of Guardians. He did not care for the manner in which they had elected members that night, and he thought it would be far better if the ratepayers of the township had an opportunity of electing their representatives by a vote at an election. The CHAIRMAN: That is quite right. Every individual is at liberty to do as he like€. All that has been done here to-night is that the members of each association have under- taken to ask their respective parties to support the nomina- tions made here to-night. (Hear, hear, and applause.) On the motion of Mr. BEECH, seconded by Mr. RATCLIFFE 3 Vote of tbanke w 35 tendered to the retiring members of the Local Board and Board of Guardians. A vote of thanks was accorded to the Ch al-man on the proposal of Mr. CARLILE, seconded by Mr. HEYES, and the meeting concluded.

unwise proceeding, and. that the inhabitants were at the present moment reaping the fruits of that wayward policy. 4 (Loud applause.)--Mr. Curzons, who had previously given 1 indications of his opposition to the scheme, here interposed . with the remark : 'You will have to prove that," amid loud cries of "shut up" and "turn him out." Mr. Curzons: I am a ratepayer and have a right to speak. (Disorder.) I like people when they make assertions to prove them. ("Put him out," and loud hisses.) You have always found me too straightforward to have any underhand work, and we know very well there are gentle- men on the platform—(the conclusion of the sentence was lost in a great uproar of voices )—Dr. MacDorGam, stid it WAS not worth while taking any notice of him (Mr. Curzans), and asked the audience to keep their temper and leave him alone. He would mention two circumstances with that undertaking which he thought every workingman and every individual between Runcorn and Liverpool must be familiar with. For a considerable time there had been a "talk" about a carriage road to Widnes—they had heard it talked of at public meetings and at the Board of Com- missioners—but the great fact that the policy adopted at the period to which he'had alluded was fatal to the very ex- istence of a carriage road was lost sight of. A carriage road to Whines would have been formed ere this had Run- corn been friendly, instead of hostile, opponents to the scheme—(applause)—and he thought it must be apparent to everybody that the company would have agreed to con- , s Eruct a carriage road as it was feasible enough at that I time. The next question in connection with that scheme was the pontage on the bridge. The pontage at one time was id., but it had been reduced a fraction or two in the third-class, and that charge was imposed through an omis- sion on the part of the people opposing the scheme. They had also to pay a heavy freight of charges for passing from Runcorn to Widnes. Ile was not going to raise the question of the expensiveness or otherwise of the bridge. The people of Runcorn thought proper to take their own course, and the result was they had no carriage road and the burden of a heavy pontage, which it rested with the directors of the company to reduce to what he called fair charges, such as were the charges on equal lengths of other railway districts. (Applause.) He offered these illustrations to show what was likely to be established by opposition to the canal. He referred to the statement 1 that ths promoters proposed to take ships of 4,000 and 5,000 tons to Manchester, and remarked that at the present they \ could not bring vessels of more than 350 or 400 tons burden 1 to Runcorn. If the promoters choosed to spend their money- in deepening the estuary of the Mersey to establish corn- , munication between Liverpool and Manchester, it could not be done without labour, and he asked where WAS there a township or port in any part of the district more centrally situated than Runcorn. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Run- corn was the place where the greater part of the money would be spent in, and where much labour would be em- ployed in the gigantic undertaking. He went on to say that in asking for that petition the promoters wished them to do nothing which would compromise the position of Runcorn. If one foot of water was added to the present depth it meant so much more trade for Runcorn and Weston Point, and if the canal Was made, what would the result be? He asked a friend of his who was particularly interested in the salt trade what the effect would be upon that trade. He replied that it would revolutionise it. rrobably they were not aware that half a million tons of salt went every year from Liverpool to different parts of the globe, but if the canal were made, every pound hf that would be shipped from Runcorn and Weston Point, for it was not likely the salt proprietors would pay the heavy dock dues at Liverpool. —Mr. CunzoNs : It's all bosh. (Cries of "Shut up," and 'Turn him out," and disturbance.)—The CHAIRMAN : Now, Mr. Curzon!, you must behave yourself. If you wish to speak afterwards you can.—Mr. Curzons essayed to speak, but his voice was drowned in the uproar, and Dr. MACDOUGALL said he should ask him to retire if he did not behave himself.—Mr. CURZONS : I am not going to have sand thrown in my eyes. (Disturbance.)—Dr.MacDonuar,L, continuing, said it stood to reason that if the salt proprie- tors could get accommodation at Weston Point and Run- corn they would not take the trouble to take their salt to Liverpool. These were facts it would be well to consider, , and he hoped Runcorn would not stand in its own light. He referred to the few privileges which Runcorn possessed as a port, observing that the Bridgewater Navigation Com- pany Was really the port of Runeorn, but the Board of Commissioners when it was constituted the port sanitary authority had the privilege of looking after its own port arrangements without being tacked on to any riparian authority such as Liverpool on the proposed port of Manchester. The Bridgewater Navigation Company, , the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, and the , Mersey Commissioners would look well after their , own interests, and he did not think it would !be to the interest of the Manchester ship c mal ' to promote anything that would be injurious to Runcorn. He again pointed out that in supporting the petition they were not compromising any rights they possessed, and said ; ' the promoters would perhaps have an opportunity of statirw , their case on its merits this session, and Runcorn would reap a benefit from the canal so much earlier. (Applause.) . . Mr. HORSPALL seconded the motion. 1

Mr. ROBERT SHAW then ascended the platform, and said he had listened attentively to what had been stated to the meeting, and he had not heard a single reason why they ought to vote for this resolution. He was afraid the doctor's memory was very defective with regard to what ltd been done in Runcorn some years ago. There was a great parallel between the introduction of the railway into Runcorn and of the proposed canal scheme. The leading gentlemen in the town were in a great measure supporters of the railway scheme ;—they were afraid of opposing it, foolishly thinking that the London and North-Western Rail- way Company were going to put a railway through Runcorn for the benefit of the inhabitants. The directors never intended any such thing. They brought the railway for their own benefit—(hear, hear, and applause)—and the only person who opposed the company was Mr. Falk. But the local authorities of Runcorn said " Let us have this coin- pany, they will do us such a great deal of good." The com- pany did add nine miles of rails between Runcorn and Liv rpool, and ever since the people had been suffering, whereas if the scheme had been opposed the town would have had her rights. (Applause.) They had heard a great deal of talk, but very little argument, why they ought to sup- port the canal scheme. Be s Aid candidly that if they were to be benefited by the the canal scheme it was the duty of every person in Runcorn to support it. But all the promoters at present showed was that a canal was to be formed from behind Wigg Bros. and Steele's works to Man- chester; they did not show what they intended to do below Runcorn. (Hear, hear and applause.) If Runcorn was going to be benefited, then everyone, including the Bo ird of Commissioners, would be anxious to support the scheme, but at present they did not know what would take place, and he was surprised the doctor should be so bold as to ask them to take a step before they knew what was to be done at Runcorn. At present they were in the dark, and for them to take the step suggested in ignorance would be the most suicidal thing they could do. (Hear, hear.) They did not know to what expense they might be putas regarded the drainage and sewerage of the town in consequence of this scheme. The scheme would greatly affect Warrington, but that tcwn would also be greatly benefited, and the people were prepared and rightly to sacrifice a , great deal. But in Runcorn they were uncertain. He refused to support this scheme for the same reason as the Examiner, that the promoters had not complied with the requirements of the law, and because he wished to know how his own town was to he affected. He contended that ' the people would be no worse off in consequence of the Bill being delayed twelve months, and remarked that if they passed the resolution before them, that it would be used as an instrument agiinst them. The promoters would say that the very people on the river bank where the canal commenced were not afraid of the scheme, though they were in ignorance of what was going to be done. (Ap- plause.) He should not vote fur the resolution, and he advised the meetiLg to give a decided negative. (Ap- plause.)
The CHAARMAN intimated that Mr. Riley was prepared to answer any questions that might be asked.
Mr. SHAW pointed out that the canal company were not bound by anything Mr. Riley said, but only by their own plans.
Dr. M&CDOUGALL said he thought, after gontlemen had had their say, it would be much better if the guidance of the business was left in the hands of the chairman. Mr. SHAW : I am asking a question.

Dr. MAODOUGALL said if anyone present wished to ask a question upon- any particular point which might have cropped up in the ambiguous speech of Mr. ShSw, he had no doubt Mr. Riley would have pleasure in answering it. Mr. Rovr.E asked if Mr. Riley had got any petition from any towns between Warrington and Liverpool. Mr. AMPS replied in the negative, but remarked that the reason was very plain, for Runcorn was the place where the canal commenced, therefore it was unnecessary to procure petitions from places further down the river. The river being a tidal river, was in the hands of conservators for the Crow:, who would take care that the led of the river was not improperly interfered with. Mr. Leader Williams had authorised him to tell the meeting that the deep channel would come alongside the present quays of Runcorn, so that the largest vessels might come up the canal and lead and un- load at tLeir own quays—(applause)—at all states of the tide. Replying to Mr. Shaw, he observed that it was impossible to deposit plans of the work to be done between Runcorn and Liverpool, owing to the shifty nature of the channel. The engineers would not pledge themselves to say where the draining walls had to be placed, but the plans, as they ware made from time to time, of the works in the estuary of the Mersey would have to be submitted for the sanction of vari- ous bodies interested in the river, and it therefore followed that nothing would be allowed to be done that would be de- trimental to the towns on its banks. Mr. SHAW remarked that the conservators of the river had power to control the river under the Act of Parliament at present, but they would not have that power under the Act sought to be obtained by the promoters of the ship canal. •

After a few remarks from Mr. Herbert Birch, Mr. Curzons ascended the platform, and leisurely filled a tumbler which stood on the table with water, of which he imbibed a con- siderable quantity, amid tumultous laughter. Amid a loud disturbance he-proceeded to deliver an address, prefacing his remarks by stating that he knew more about the Mersey than any other man in Runcorn. He declared that the Commissioners were justified in the action they had taken until some definite proposal as to the bed of the river was set before them. (near, hear). If the canal company were going to " drudge out "—(loud laughter)—the river, very little money would he spent in Runcorn, and if they Iticrerfcl the bed of the river 20 feet, then all Runcorn goes in "

(loud and long continued laughter, and shouts '•)f " Come, off," and " Better go to Northwich.") A scene of great uproar ensued, and although Mr. CurzonS continued his speech not a word could be heard, and. be was invited to " have another drink." He was assailed with such cries as "Here's a hobby," " Get down Jemmy," and the like, until at last he was compelled to descend to his seat in front of the platform.

Mr. H. JOHNSON asked several questions of Mr. RILEY who, in reply, said it was proposed to give a depth of water to the river at Runcorn of 20 feet at low water. Mr. JOHNSON then remarked that that was what Runcorn had been in want of for the last half century, and he alluded to the great impetus which would be given to the trade in the locality.

Dr. MACDordIS.LL said he would not pay Mr. Shaw the compliment that he did not use some argument, for he had, and simply confirmed what he (the Doctor) had alreidy stated. The opposition to the Railway Bill came from the Chamber of Commerce, and not from Mr. Falk, and they afterwards found that it cost them dear.
The motion was then pat to the vote, and carried, only six hands being held up against it.

Mr. Curtzoss then inquired "How much.further had they got?" and said the resolution was about as much use as putting a weatkercock on the top of the church." (A voice: "We can wait until it tumbles in, Jemmy." The meeting then concluded, the petition I,eing numer- ously signed.
WIDNES LOCAL IIOAIW.

The usual monthly meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday, at the offices, Alforde Chambers, under the presi- dency of Mr. F. H. Gossage. There were also present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. T. Handley, Pankhurst, Foster, Kershaw, Shuttleworth, Sadler, D. Wright, Midwood, Johnson, J. 'l'. Allen (clerk), Higginson (surveyor), and Carr (gas manager).

div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

The Rev. Canon Barclay presided over the monthly meeting held at the Commissioners Board-room, on Thurs- lay. There were also present :—Dr. MacDougall, Messrs. John Simpson, W. Handley, W. Rhodes, F. A. Lake, W. Riley, and W. Brookes (secretary).

LIBRARIAN'S REPORT. The Librarian's report showed that 1,562 books had been issued from the lending library during the month of January classified as follows :—Theology 28; philosophy, political economy, Szc., 14; history, travels, and biography, 256; science and art, 64; poetry and the drama, 31; prose, fiction, 1,073; miscellaneous, 96. £1 15s. 91 had been re- ceived as tines for undue detention of books, and ss. 81 from the sale of tickets ; total, £2 is. 50. Mr. John Simp- son had presented 17 volumes during the month.—On the motion of Dr. MACWOUGALL, seculicted by Mr. WM. HAND- LEY, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Simpson for his gift.
TILE READING ROOM QUESTION.-INTERESFING DISCUSSION.
NO RENT 3f&NIVESTO.

Mr. BnooLEs said, in accordance with the instrections lie received at the last meeting of the Committee, he wrote to Mr. George S. Hazlehurst informing him of the decision of the Committee with respect to Waterloo House, anti he had received the following reply : The Elms, Runcorn, January 20,I883.—Dear kir. Brookes, —The Commissioners were fully aware that t• adopt their committee's report involved the loss of the reading-room, as far as my offer was concerned; the committee itself was fully aware ot it before their report was printed. It was nut with use a question of expense; it would li we c.ist much more, pro- bably, to have fitted the o iniug hall than the place they have granted you. However, the whole business is now concluded. —Believe me, dear sir, sincerely yours, GEORGE 5. HAZLE- BURST.

Mr. HANDLEY inqulted if the Commissicners had formally reported the resolution at which they had arrived with reference to Waterloo House.—Mr. BROOKES: It was reported by Dr. Steele at the last meeting of the committee. There has been nothing done since by the Commissioners. —Mr. HANDLEY: What I mean is—are the Cornissioners taking steps to find us rootns in Waterloo House ?—The CHAIRMAN.—They have giyen us no formal intimation of it.—Dr. MACDOUGALL, in fairness to Mr. Hazlehurs,, related miautely the course events had taken since Mr. Hazlehurst first made his offer to the Commissioners to establish a. reading roore, concluding by saying that the Commissioners would not accept one thing nor another. They would not accept £25 a-year for the present room, nor the offer to tit up Waterloo House, which would have been equal to a gift to the ratepayers of £BO per annum for three years. But the Commissioners simply said " We will not be driven ; we will allocate three rooms ; " and they did what was worse, attempted to " pin" Mr. Hazlehurst to the offer he had made. That offer was as conditional as any offer ever made ; it extended to the two rooms which had been so often named, and no further, and he thought, in justice to Mr. Hazlehurst, who bad tried to be a philanthropist, but was not permitted to be so, through the Commissioners taking a commercial view of their duties. And the ratepayers were deprived for the next three years of the increased usefulness of a reading- room and of the Library, and the result of the action of the I Commissioners would ever be a memorial of their wisdom. There had been a great many aspersions thrown about Mr. Hazlehurst, and he thought it was only right that the bare facts ehould come bore the public.—Mr. SIMPSON said he did not think that it was desirable that this discussion should be continued much longer, bit al a member of the Free Library Comtnittee he should like to say that it was a pity that Mr. Hazlehurst did not carry out Mr. Lake's idea. The offer Was made unconditionally, and he was sure no one but thought that if Mr. Hazleherst had accepted the the recommendation of the committee which was appointed, would have been more satisfactory in the issue it to the Library Committee and •to the readers. With regard to the Commissioners he would not say that they had been as judicious in their manner as they might have been, but he thought it might have been a mistake if they had been persuaded, by the gift from Mr. Ilazlehurst for three years, to sacrifice the best room of Waterloo House—(hear, hear)—by givines it up for a read- ing-room or any other purpose, instead of retaining it as the Board-room. It would not have been satisfactory for the Commissioners to hive been on sufferance in their own Board-room, as would have been the case had they been al- lowed to make use of the reading-room for the purpose of holding their meetings. It would not, he thought, have been satisfactory if the dining-room had been used as a reading- room and also as the room in which the people who were I applying for books from the Library had to assemble and re- ceive their books. He was very sorry the thing had taken , the position it had done, and he thought that if Mr. Hazlehurst had not withdrawn his offer, but just made the best one of the rooms which the committee recommended everybody would have been satie.fied.—Mr. HANDLEY: I have been asking the question as to whether there was any near probtbility of rooms beiug offered to us I for alterAtione, so that we could And a reading- room and a room for library purposes. Mr. BROoKES said the Commissioners had taken no ! steps beyond asking the approval of Her Majesty's Treasury to the proposed appropriation of rooms at Waterloo House for the library. He supposed they would allow the question of removal to remain at rest until the commencement of the next year in March.—The CHAIRMAN: Until they get formal permission from the authorities.—Mr. BROOKES: Not necessarily. Perhaps more on account of the funds.—Mr. HANDLEY: We require the permission of the Treasury. Still that will not prevent us making any use we may of Waterloo House.—Dr. MAC- DOUGALL said the present building answered the ;purposes of the library quite well, DOW as they could not establish a reading room or news room. Therefore, to in- . ' cu the expense of removing to Waterloo Housa seemed to I .' I him, at all events for the present, to be an unwise proceed- lug. If the walls were covered with book-shelves he did not think they need remove at all.—The CHAIRMAN : There is no proposition before,the committee.—Dr. MACDOUGALL: I don't sea any advantage to be gained by removing. It is entirely a m itter for the Commissienere, and no doubt they would do it in their own way and in due course.—Mr. HANDLEY said he had mentioned the subject because there were about 300 volumes that were kept out of the Library at present—they could not be catalogu«l—owing to there not being any room for classification. This was an impor- tant matter for the readers, and it was imperative that for the good of the Library, that it should be permanently Incited soon, or that some ehelves should be made for placing the books on the walls. Otherwise, the readers could not participate to the full in the advantages which the library afforded.—Dr. MAcDouGALL Let the shelving be asked for.—Mr. HANDLEY : I scarcely like asking the Commiseionrs to incur any expense in these rooms if they are not to be our permanent location. I think we should spend money that would be nseful in providing for present and future needs in other directions. I consider that our removal to Waterloo House might be very advan- tageous to the public, and scarcely increase our expenses. I think we could meet this in s, ine, way if they allowed us the use of the rooms. I was hoping for the resolution come to by the Commissioners at their last monthly meeting would have been sent on for our discussion and approval. I rather regret that it has not, because the omission prevents us tak- ing any definite steps in the interests of the library. The CHAIRMAN said the Commissioners had done what they could in the matter. They had sent to the Treasury for approval, and there the thing stopped.—Mr. HANDLEY: And so the books are stopped. It is all at a deadlock.— Mr. LAZE remarked that the removal of the library to Waterloo House was only a question of time.—The CHAIR- MAN : But we cannot take any steps to go to Waterloo House yet.—Mr. HANDLEY : Certainly not. I quite agree . with that. Mr. SIMPSON observed that some ! alterations would be necessary in some of the : rooms if they removed to Waterloo House. Would that expense be borne by the Library Committee or the Commissioners ?—Dr. MacDoroALL : Undoubtedly by ; the Library Committee.—Mr. RHODES : I should think that permanent alterations niltuld be at the expense of the ; Commissioners.—The CritrillarAN : If we are charged a rent, it is only fair that the Commissioners should make the alterations.—Dr. MACDOUGALL said lie and Mr. Lake visited Nottingham Free Library the other day, and they took particular care to inquire if the committee paid any rent. They said they did not. When the I Commissioners made inquiries they would be informed that no rent was charged to any free library.-1 \fr. HANDLEY: There is no rent charged at Warrington ; aor anywhere.—ln reply to a question from Mr. Simpson,l Dr. MAcDounALL said the Nottingham Free Library was in the new Uroiversity buildings belonging to the Corporation. I —The CHAIRMAN said the question of rent was not before I the Committee, and Mr. HANDLEY remarked that the ques- tion had arisen in consequence of a mistake in the reading of the Act.—After deciding that the words "H. F. L" j shell(' he upan the beck of each volume, the Committee't p:oce«l !Pg., COL' c!udeci.

div.head: :WARD QUESTION.
div.p: THE :WARD QUESTION.

Each member was supplied with a report giving the re- sult of the inquiries made of a number of towns with regard to the working of districts divided into wards.—The CHAIR- MAN said each member had as much information on this question as himself, and it appeared to him from his perusal of the report, that no Board had voluntarily divided their districts into wards but were compelled to do so in conse- quence of certain alterations made in their mode of govern- ment. So far as he could make out some of the answers to the inquiries were vague, and some were no answers at all; but many of the bodies wrote as if they would prefer to go back to the old system. He must say that he did not see that the %1' idnes Local Eoard was not a thoroughly representative body under the present system, and he could not imagine how dividing the town into wards would make it more representative. Each member was responsible for what went en at the Board, and he could not discern any advantage that would be gained by the proposed divi- sion.—Mr. SALLER iuquired whether if the town was divided into wards, it would not he easier for the people who wished to claim their votes before the returning officer to do so? At the last election there were hundreds of people turned away, and they conld not get a vote at all.—The CHAIRMAN replied that he did not Lee that it would. They would have to form a number of committees, and where they had a num- ber of people trying to do the same thing it was seldom accomplished so well as where they had a few persons who were thoroughly up in the work and gave their time to it. The case mentioned by Mr. Sadler had arisen, he thought, through the ratepayers neglecting to look after the registra- tion of their votes. For a long time they did not trouble themselves about registration at all, and then when an elec- tion time arrived they found they shad no power to vote. He thought the two associations—the Ratepayers' Association and the Owners and Occupiers' Association— would alter that state of things very much.— Mr. SADLER remarked that at the last election it was impossible for the returning officer to give votes to all persons who were entitled to one. Time would not allow him ; in fact hundreds could not get their vote in con- sequence of time not being sufficient.—The CHAIRMAN: What do you mean ?—Mr. SADLER: I mean to say that the relieving officer had not time to look into cases to see whether certain people were entitled to a vote or not. —Mr. KERSHAW pointed out that voting papers were distributed four days previous to the election, and it was entirely a person's own fault if he did not obtain a vote.—Mr. HANDLEY said he understood that if the town were divided, the same returning officer would preside over all the wards. The ex-chairman of the Northwich Local Board had informed him that the same persons took the papers from the same wards on the same day, so that it would not alter their arrangements at all.—The CHAIRMAN observed that Mr. Allen had pointed out to him that all a ward committee could do would be to see that there was a list prepared showing how many v3ters there were in each ward. The two associations could do that now. He remarked, in reply to an observation by Mr. Sadler, that every facility ought to be provided for persons voting, and it was the intention of. the Local Government Board that it should be so.—Mr. WRIGHT : If we get more information upon the subject we can bring it up at some future time.—The CHAIRMAN: Quite so. I don't see any objection to that at all. You all mustagree with me that as far as this report goes it is six of one and half a dozen of the other.—Mr. WRIGHT : It is so in this case.—lt was then resolved that the report lie on the table.

div.head: LEVEL CROSSING NUISANCE.
div.p: THE LEVEL CROSSING NUISANCE.

The following memorial was read : January 27, 18S3.—To the Chairman and Members of the Widnes L- cal Board.--Gentlemen,—Promsed abolition of the railway level crossing in Newtown —We, the undersigned, owners and ; c:nwiers of property in Newtown, having seen the plan in connection with the above, which was appioved at your meeting on the 9th inst., beg respectfully to express our approval of the same, and s;rcerely trust that you will use your be,t effort.; to have the said plan carried out. Kindly permit us to say that we should be glad if the foptbridge can be re- tained. _(Signatures follow
The CHAIRMAN remarked that this matter would probably be discussed at the public mvting to be held on the 21st Inst.; and no discussion uow took place.
A STOPPED SEWER.- CLAIM FOR DAMAGES BY A. MEMBER.
The CLERK read the following:—

Widt ei, February 12th. 1883.T0 the Ciairman Widnes Local Board. Detr sir,—We herewith hatfd you a claim. To stoppage of our works in c ,nsequence of drainage from the saw mill cellar being stopped, throogh the main sewer in HutcWn- son-street and Dock-road being tilled up to the arch. We esti- mate our damage At £250. See our letters to yoursurveyor.— Yours most truly, W. H. KERSHAW and Co.
The CHAIRMAN remarked that they could not consider this claim per se, and he suggested that it bc referred to the Highway Committee. The suggestion was adopted.

div.head: PARLIAMENTARY OPPOSITION.
div.p: PARLIAMENTARY OPPOSITION.

On the motion of Mr. KERSHAW, seconded by Mr. MID- WOOD, Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., Warringtcn, were ap- pointed solicitors to the Board during the special Parliamen- tary opposition to the Bill of the London and North-Western Railway Company.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF RETURNING OFFICER.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF RETURNING OFFICER.
On the motion of Mr. HANDLEY, the Chairman was una- nimoubly elected returning officer during the ensuing elec- tion.
GAS COMMITTEE.

The Gas and Water Committee's minutes contained the engineer's report, which stated that the water in stock on January 17th 1883, was 5,337,346 gallons ; the illu- minating power of the gas during the month had averaged 15-72 candles; the wages required during the coming four weeks were £7O per week for gas and water works; the month's accounts amounted to £577 lOs 5d for gas works, £133 Os 2d for water, works. Dr. Campbell Brown bad made an analysis of the water at Netherly and Stocks' well, and certified that both samples were excellent for domestic purposes. A recommendation was passcd that water meter testing apparatus be obtained, the cost to be about £3O. A letter, dated 30th January, was read from L. and N.-W.R. Co., asking terms for supply of water to Gatehouse, Johnson's Crossing, Cuerdly. Instructions were given that it be supplied on the usual terms. Another letter was read, dated let January, from Mr. T. Heald, offer- ing to continue the tenancy of Pex Hill shooting at present rent, £5 per annum, payable in advance, and subject to six months' notice on either side. Recommended that it be ac- cepted. It was recommended that an insurance be effected with the Employers' Liability Act Insurance to cover any risks, at the rate of 2s. per £lOO of wages paid. . .
The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Pank- burst. It was decided to advertise the shooting on Pex Hill.
HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.-THE REV. FATHER FINEGAN MEETS
WITH AN OUSTRUCTION.

At a meeting of the Highway Committee on the 9h ult.. Mr. Kershaw reported that Mr. Worthington was inclined to recommend his directors to adopt the suggestions of this committee by forming a road into Ann-street, but with a different gradient to that suggested.—Letter read, dated 17th January, from London and North-Western Railway Corn- pany, stating that the saggestions about the windows in the huts at Appleton and Plumpton Crossings will be carried out.—LAter read, dated 18th January, the surveyor reported the repairs had been done to footpaths at Moss Bank and Ann-street by S. and M. Railway Company.—Letter read, dated 9th January, frpm Mr. T. Hulse, reporting wilful damage to the seats. The surveyor instructed to find out, if possible, and prosecute the kffenders.—Letter read, dated 31st January. from Mr. G. Grauthorp, asking when the work, as per agreement, will be done to Moorfield-lane. The clerk instructed to reply that the matter will be considered when preparing the next estimate in March next.—Letter read, dated Ist February. from Mrs. Duxbury, asking for some flagging and curbing to be done to Church-street, Farnworth, as agreed upon, in consideration of the frontage being Eet back. The surveyor instructed to do the work.— Letter read, dated Ist February. from Messrs. W. H. Ker- shaw and Company, complaining of damage done by the stoppage of the sewer in Dock-road. Consideration deferred, pending inspection.—Letter read, dated 31st January, from Mr. Greaves, asking for the flagging to be done as agreed ! upon to Widnes-road and Greenfield-street. The surveyor instructed to do the work.—Letter read, dated 22nd January, from Rev. T. Finegan (the surveyor having called upon him to do some repairs), stating that, through an obstruction erected by Mr. Kershaw, he cannot get a cart along to do the necessary repairs to footpath—Simm's Cross to Apple- ton. The surveyor instructed to reply that the Board has nothing to do with Mr. Kershaw's obstruction, and request the repairs to be made —The committee inspected Hutchin- son-street and West Bank sewers, and found them full of solid refuse, also Messrs. Kershaw and Company's yard, and I found the drains completely blocked up. The surveyor was instructed to press forward the cleaning as the stoppage is doing great damage to the surrounding property.—The Iminutes were passed on the proposition of Mr. KERSHAW, seconded by Mr. SHurrrxwoarrar.

THE SEWERAGE SCHEME. ENGINEER AND CONTRACTOR IN DISPUTE.—MR. 3IIDWOOD ON THE "WAR PATH." At a special meeting held on the 15th ult.. a letter was read from the resident engineer to the chairman of the Com- mittee asking for advice. The reply which bad been sent was approved. The resident engineer was instructed to write to the contractor to go on with the works, and likewise to call his attention to the unsatisfactory progress he was making with the work, and the dangerous state of part of it. On the sth inst. the committee met at the sewer, inspected the work, and heard various complaints from Mr. Jeffreys. The resident engineer was unable to be present through illness, and the consideration of complaints deferred. The resident engineer's report was read as follows :—" The present state of affairs in connection with these works are, briefly, that the contractor has not carried out the instructions which I have given him, and has made several excuses for net doing so. Up to the 20th ult, the wcrk executed by the contractor amounts to £32 6s 10d. This I have not issued a certificate for, as the damage done to the neighbouring property will cost considerably more than this to rectify, and until I re- ceive your instructions to the contrary, I shall not certify until the amount of damage is compensated for by the value of work done, and not paid for, or until the contractor satis- factorily makes good the damage. The contractor has made application for permission to proceed with the work in Dit- ton-roail. Under the present circumstan zes, I do not con- sider it will be advisable to gri:e him r.cl permission, us he

has two trenches open, and in a dangerons state, and is not proceeding with the work with such diligence as is nocessary to avoid accidents, and complete the contract in the given time. I shall be glad of your instructions hereon. lam still confined to my bed, suffering from rheumatism." Letters complaining of interference with drainage works were read from Mr. J. C. Routledge, Messrs. Snape and Co., and Messrs. Golding, Davies and Co. Messrs. R. Davies and Co. wrote with respect to the arbitration case, suggest- ing that only two professional valuers be employed on each side as mentioned by Messrs. Part and Co. The suggestion was agreed to.—Mr. KERSHAW moved and Mr. PANICHURST seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. MIDWOOD in- quired if the Board had any contract with Mr. Hancock for the supplying of brick work. He understood there was not a contract, and yet the Board was paying large sums of money to him monthly. He also desired to know if a letter had been received from Major Cross respecting the main outlet sewer, in which he said he would hold the Board responsible for certain damage caused through a defect. He thought it was of the greatest importance that the Board should be aware of such a letter from Major Cross, who was the promoter of the scheme.—The CLERK remarked that the letter referred to was received after the last committee meeting, and would not therefore come before the Board. He read, however, the following commu- nication from Major Cross:— "February 6th, 1882 —There is a further leakage from our sewer into your excavations north-west of Golding. Davies, and Co.'s Office, and also very evident signs of depression in the lines of rails passing over the place. You will please note that I shall hold your Board entirely responsible for all drainage accruing as well for what has already been done through the defective protection of the trustees (Hutchinson) property." February 7th. 1883.—1 want to make an open ditch along the west side of Marsh Brook to intercept the drainage from the waste banks and fluid. Your contractor has put a quan- tity of clay on the site opposite the south-west end of the Widnes Metal Company's works. I shall he glad if you will give instructions for its removal at once and oblige." Mr. Minwooto had no suggestion to make with regard to the letters, but looking at the state of the sewer he did not think it wise to allow anything to come to the Board unnoticed.— The CHAIRMAN said there was nothing inherently wrong in the scheme.—Mr. Minwoon : I fear we shall find it to be so, sir.—Mr. KERSHAW, replyiag to Mr. Handley, said the surveyor was in charge of the sewerage work during the illness of the engineer, and informed Mr. Midwood there was a contract with Mr. Hancock. He remarked that there was nothing wrong in the letters from Major Cross, who was not debarred from making a complaint whether he was a promoter of the scherneor not. He was a trustee of Hut- chinson's estate, and he was working in their interest. Mr. Midwood went a little too far when he entered into such criticisms.—The CHAIRMAN, referring to the illness of the resident engineer, said the contractor had not in conse- quence of that illness to stop the work. It was his duty to go on with the work without orders.—Mr. KERSHAW explained that the dispute arose between the engineer and the contractor, because the former refused to do a piece of new work before he had remedied a bad piece of old work. The specifications and everything connected with the sewer were perfectly clear, and the Board had nothing to fear; but to make the contractor do the work in a proper manner.— The CHAIRMAN pointed out to the surveyor that he had the power to settle any dispute, and then to make a representa- tion to the Board through the committee.—Mr. KERSHAW said the matter was as plain as AB C. The surveyor only need give the resident engineer and contractor notice to proceed with the work. "Jeffries had brought it upon himself."—Mr. MIDWOOD observed that if Mr. Kershaw was spending his own n:oney on the scheme he would not take matters so 'calmly. (Hear, hear.)—The CHAIRMAN sug- gested that the committee should hold a special meeting and deal fully with tile subject in dispute.—Mr. MIDWOOD proceeded to make some remarks with reference to the con- tract for bricks, when he was interrupted by Mr. KERSHAW, who said the contract was not between the Board and Mr. Hancock.—Mr. MIDWOOD protested excitedly against Mr. Kershaw's contradictory statements. Mr. KERSHAW (warmly) : Will you allow me to explain myself? Don't eat me.—Mr. MIDWOOD: I should be sorry to do that. (Loud laughter.)—Mr. KERSHAW then explained Mr. Han- cock was simply carrying out Mr. Kirk's contract, and the Board was actually liable for the payment of it.—Mr. MID- WOOD : I think yo.o will see Mr. Kershaw's opinion is worth nothing at all. (Mr. Kershaw: Hear. hear.) We are bound as a Board to have a contract for any expenditure over £lOO, and here we are paying hundreds of pounds without any contract arall. There is £lO7 this month.—Mr. SHUT- TLEWORTH : I should like to know something before I sign this cheque. I have got a cheque before me for £167 16s. —Mr. KERSHAW: I am not a solicitor; and Mr. Midwood says we cannot pay.—Mr. MIDWOOD: I appeal to the Chairman. If he rules differently I have finished. I think it is important that the members should know what they were signing. We shall have a surcharge Mr. Chairman.— Mr. KERSHAW then moved that the minutes be .referred back for further consideration.—Mr. I'ANKHURST seconded the motion which was carried.

HEALTH COMMITTEE: THE DISPOSAL OF DISEASED CARCASES. On the Bth ult. the members of the Health Committee made a general inspection of the sanitary condition of the town. The Medical Officer reported that during the month of January there had been 104 births and 44 deaths, representing a birth rate of 49.92 per I,ooo,and a death rate of 2112 per 1,000. Of the deaths 12 were of children under one year, and seven of children between one year and five. Zymotic diseases accounted for three. The nuisance inspector repotted that there had been two fatal cases of measles and one of typhoid fever; three houses had been disinfected. The market superintendent reported that the receipts for last month were £l7 45.• Bd., being an increase of 6s. Id. as compared with January 1882. Five shops were now let. The stalls had let very well during the month, but the receipts from the fair ground were less than last month, owing to the wet weather. The number of beasts and pigs killed in the slaughter-house had not been so large as in the previous month.—Mr. PANKHURST moved, and Mr. WRIGHT seconded the adoption of the minutes.—A discus- sion arose as to the seizure of the diseased carcase of a cow, belonging to Mr. Mooney, who had purchased it a few days previously at the Liverpool market for £l7 10s. It was alleged that it had been sold by-the nuisance inspector to Mr. Edward Percy, and Mr. Mrnwoop asked how the Board were to know it had not been used for human food. He also thought, in justice to Mr. Mooney, that any sum that was realised ought ta be banded over to him.—Mr. Dixow said the usual custom had been followed in this case. The cow, had been seized and dealt with according to the Public Health Act. He knew that the cow was not used as human food. Mr. Midwood had insinuated that he was benefited by the sale of the carcase, but he wished to say distinctly that he had not; the proceeds went to the committee.—The minutes were passed. THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN.—MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNUAL REPORT.

The Medical Officer's report for the year ending December last had been approved by the Health Committee, and ordered to be printed. It read as follows : Gentlemen,—The number of deaths registered during the past year, in the township cf Widnes was .514. and calculating on a population of 25,000 persons, this gives a death rate of 23 56 per thousand of population for that year. From the princ'pal zymotic diseases 78 deaths were recorded, which gives a death rate of 3.12 rer thousand of population from that class of diseases They were as follows :—Measles 12, scarlatina 15. diphtherial, whooping cough 2, typhus fever 1, tyr hold fever 9, diarrhcea 38-78. Although this rate is much higher than that for zymotic disflases in 1881. it compares favourably with that rate for 1880, which was 352 per thousand. 1881 vas an exceptionally healthy year as far as this townsh'p was con- cerned. The deaths of children under one year (including premature births) numbered 171, or 6 8i per thousand of popu- lation, and those of children between 1 and 5 years 134, or 5 36 per thousand. The following table epitomises the ages at which the deaths occurred thronzhout the township grouped in accordance with the ages fixed in the tables furnished by the Local Government Board. whlch are duly filled up and accom- pony the report. Deaths of persons under 1 year 17', over 1 and under 5 years 134, over 5 and under 15 years 22, over 15 and under 25 years 23, over 25 and under 60 years 117. over 60 years 47—total of all ages 514. The births during 1882 num- bet ed 1,087. giving a birth rate of 42 68 per thousand of popu- lation. I will now refer briefly to the outbreaks of zymotic diseases during the year, and the steps taken to art eat the spread of such diseases. Small Pox: No case of this disease occurred during the year in the township. Scarlatina: There were 15 fatal cases of scarlatina during 1882; they t 'sok place chiefly in the autumn, and were not confined to any particular locality. I visited the various infected houses, but could not discover any special cause for the outbreak. This disease was prevalent in many parts of England during the autumn months. The Sanitary Inspector carefully disinfected all the houses where the disease occurred, and no child from any such house was allowed to return to school for a period of three months, dating from the commencement of the disease. Measles: There were 12 fatal cases of measles during the year, almost all of children under five years old, and occurring during the autumn; as in the case of the last-named d'sease no special causes for the out- break could be disvvered and similar means to prevent the spread of disease were employed, with the exception that children were allowed to return to aeho,l at the end of one month instead of three months. Typhoid and Typhus Ferer : Nine eases of typhoid and one typhus fever proved fatal. Several other cases of the former disease were reported to me, and means were taken to remedy the drainage where it was found defective, to drain off stagnant water. and generally to improve th., sanitary condition of the neighbourhood in which the disease appeared Diphtheria: Only cne fatal ease occurred, and it is supposed to have been cansed by defective drainage. The drainage is now in good condition. Diarrhaa: There were 38 fatal cases of this disease, 36 being of children under five years; 31 of these deaths vccurred ?ming the months of July, August. and September, due probably to the usual causes, namely. sour food, unripe and over-ripe fruit, which are peculiarly productive of this &gape in warm weather. Whooping Cough: Two fatal cases were recorded. Public Works: The contracts for the main sewerage of ft great portion of the township. mentioned in my report for 1881, are being carried out as rapidly as weather and other circumstances will permit. but are not yet ccmpleted. Water Supply: The whole town- ship is abundantly supplied with pure water. Scavenging: The scavenging has not been carried out in the efficient manner I could wish, but I have represented this matter to my Board. and they have changed their night soil contractor, and engaged one who will. I hope, carry out his work in a more satisfactory manner. The accompanying statement by the Sanitary In- spector gives the particulars of work done during 1882.—1 am. gentlemen, faithfully yours, WILLIAM COOPER.

THE INSPECTOR'S REPORT FOR THE YEAR. The following is the Inspector's report of the sanitary work for the year ending December 31st, 1882 : Notices served, and complied with, to abate drainage and other nuisances, 28 ; houses closed as unfit for habitation, 16 : animals kept so as to be a nuisance, 13; houses disinfected, 46; ashpits and privies cleaned. 4,620; ashpits and privies taken down and rebuilt, 23; ashpits and privies repaired, 18 ; eizures of meat and fish (including one carcase of cow, five Pigs, 2 cwts, of bacan, and 31 cwts. fish), unfit for human food. ; seizures of fruit and vegetables (including 18 cwts. of apples, 4 cwts. of onions, 1 cwts. of turnips, and 2,800 oranges), unfit for human food, 25 ; meat, fruit, and milk cases which were brought before the magistrates, and (except in one case), conviction with penalty ob'ained 4. The Markets and Taira Temporary Order of 1583. Notice is het eby given, that a Public Sale, or Market, for the sale of fat swine, will be held on Wednesday next, the 21st inst., at Town Hill, Warrington, subject to the following condi- tions : (i) Swine exposed at such sale shall, after th.tir arrival thereat, and before they are moved therefrom, be marked by and at the expense of the owner, consignee' sir other person expos- ing them, by the painting or stamping of the letter NI, about six inches long, on the left side of such of the swine with the following composition, namely :—Rosin, five parts; oil of tur- pentine, two parts: and blue or red ochre, one part; melted and used warm; or with some other adhesive composition of a blue or red colour. (ii) Every animal that is exposed at such ssle, whether it is sold thereat or not, shall be slaughtered within s'x days after the day on which the sale is held, (iii) Animals exposed at such sale shall not afterwards be ex- posed at any other public sale, except at the Metropolitan Market under the special provisions specified in Article 7of this Order. WM. HENRY BROOK, n wn Clerk. Dated this 16th February, 1883.

TH E ASTLEY COTTON MILL, COMPANY, LIMITEP, DURINFIELD.—To be. incorporated under the 0. mpanies Acts of 1862, 1867, and 1877, whereby the lia- bility of shareholders is limited to the amount of shares. Capital £lOO,OOO, in 20 900 shares of £5 each. Payable $1 per share on /application. and 5i per share on allotment. Further calls will not exceed 5s per share, and will be made at intervals of not less than one month. If no allotment be made, the amount paid on application will be returned in full. PROVISIONAL COMMII TEE. Mr A. C. Boyd. The Lakes, Dukinfield chairman Mr John Ashworth, The Likes, Dukinfield Mr Ralph Bates. Acres Bank, Stalybridge Mr John Mocksage, Dewsnap House. Stoney, Ashton-under-Lyne Mr John Storrs, Brookside, Mottram-road, Staly bridge Mr John Sykes, Astley•street, Dukinfield Mr Marvellous Webster. Turner-lane, Ashton-under-Lyne Mr Emor G. Wrigley, Victoria-place, Dukinfield BANKERS. The Manchester and Liverpool District Banking Company, Limited. SOLICITOR. Mr T Alfred Garforth, Dukintield (who will act as Secretary pro. tern). A P.O lIITECTS. Messrs Potts. Pickup, and Dixon. Oldham and Manchester. Ps ospectuses and to ms of application for shares can be obtained from the bank and all its branches, or from the solicitor on and after Monday. February Twelfth, 1883. PROSPECTUS. 1 The Company is formed for the purpose of erecting and wos king in Dukinfield a first-class fire-proof Cotton Mill of the m it approved design, dimensions, and arrangements, with engines and machinery and mode at driving cmstructed upon the latest and best pi inciples. 2. The Mill will contain 80,000 spindles, In about equal pro. portions of twist and weft, and all necessary preparation. 3. A most eligible site has been offered in Uppet King street, bounded on the south side by Piektord-lane, and arrangements have been made for an abundant sopply of wate- suitable for boiler purposes, free of charge. This land is offered by the trustees of the late Mr. Astley's estate at the very low rate of Id per yard chief rent, cApltalized at 20 years' purchase, and the amount will ha taken in shares. 4. It is estimated that the Mill and Premises can be erected and filled with the most modern machinery at a toe of within 20s per spindle, or about 5s per spindle under the present market value of many of the best Oldham mills. This will make a difference of £2O, 00 in favour of the propisred New Mill, in addition to the saving in land and water. 5. The township of Dukinfield posssases facilities for coal supply, and canal and railway carriage. unsurpassed by any Is-cal ty in the neighbourhood r and xis plot of land in the dis- trict offers such conspicuens advantages for mill purposes as the proposed site. 6. The cotton industry is at present well employed, and prospects both for home and export trades are good; white the cost of building and machinery being low renders this a fitting opportunity for an undertakieg of this nature 7. The Directors do not expect to call up more than £2 10s per shire. 8. No contracts of any kind will be entered into by the Pro- visional Committee, but a meeting of Shareholders for for the election of directors. sic., will be called immediately the state of the Share List warrants this step , 9. On review of these and other circumstances, investois will be able to see that this undertaking offers sound security, w th prospects of sustantial dividends. 10. A large number of shares have been already spoken for, and the Provisional Committee trust that intending investors will make immediate application in order that the Company may be registered at once, and building operations carried on during the ensuing summer months. 11. It is proposed to allow interest on all calls after the rate of 1.15 per cent., until such time as the mill gets to work.

Several addresses were delivered;-1 and an entertainment was given by the young folks. ST. VALENTIA'S DAY AT WIDNES.—As was to be expected, a largo influx of missives took place at Widnes post office on Tuesday and Wednesday. It is estimated that on the former day 2,700 valentines were posted at the head office and the receiving boxes; and on Wednesday 3,200 were received for delivery. The numbers show an increase of 500 over last year. FARNWORTH TEMPERANCE AND TOTAL ABSTINENCE SOCIETY.—The junior section of this society gave an enter- tainment in the girls' school-room, Yarnworth, on Tuesday evening. The Rev. Joseph Holden presided, and there was a crowded attendance. An excellent programme was gone through in good style; and Mr. James Mercer, prisongate missionary, Liverpool, and the Rev. George Bpd, the vicar, delivered addresses. WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONARY SOCIETY: MEETING- AT WIDNES.—The annual meeting of Widnes Branch of the Wesleyan Home Missionary Society was held in Victoria- road chapel on Tuesday evening. Mr. Joseph Robinson presided, and there was a good audience. The annual re- port, read. by Rev. J. Tessyinan, showed that the receipts in the Widnes district amounted to £l6. The Rev. R. Oderry (of Liverpool), Rev. J. Harper (superintendent minister) &livered' addresses. The usual votes of thanks were passed. HERR COHEN AT RUNCORN.—This distinguised phrenolo' gist continues to attract large audiences by kis excellent lectures in the Public Hall. On Tuesday evening he made a departure from the usual course, delivering a lecture on the subject of "The manners and customs of the Jewe." The Rev. W. Preston presided, and delivered an address. Herr Cohen described in a graphic and eloquent style the various customs of his fellow-countrymen, and the manner in which he was coverted to Christianity. His discourse was listened to with great attention. ARRESTED ON SUSPICION.—At Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, before Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, Thos. Thompson was charged, on suspicion, with stealing a suit of clothes, the property of the Wrexham Union. On the previous day the prisoner went into the police office, and asked for a ticket for a night's lodgings, but as he was wearing a suit of Union clothing he was detained. Enquiries were made, and the Wrexham authorities forwarded a telegram stating that the clothing was given to the prisoner because he ha, none of his own.—Prisoner was discharged.
